articles.title: Families demand Mexico reveal full details of military role in disappearance of 43 students
articles.summary: The families of the victims in one of Mexico’s most infamous atrocities say it’s time for the Claudia Sheinbaum government to release all of the information it holds about the role the military…

image.caption: Students from the Raúl Isidro Burgos Rural Teacher-Training College in Ayotzinapa, Guerrero, prepare to take part in a march on Saturday in Mexico City marking the 12th anniversary of the disappearance of 43 students from the college. (Jorge Barrera/CBC)

blocks.text: The families of the victims in one of Mexico's most infamous atrocities say it's time for the government of President Claudia Sheinbaum to release all of the information it holds about the role the military played in the disappearance of 43 students from a teachers' college in Ayotzinapa, Guerrero.

Thousands marched along one of Mexico City's main thoroughfares on Saturday to the National Palace, in the capital’s historic centre, to mark the 12th anniversary of the students’ disappearance from the all-male school.
"Everything points to the military," said Maria de Jesus Tlatempa, the mother of José Eduardo Bartolo Tlatempa, one of the 43, who was 19 years old when he vanished.

Tlatempa and the other fathers, mothers, uncles and siblings of the 43 led the march, which began in the shadow of Mexico City’s iconic Angel of Independence monument, ringed on Saturday by steel fencing.

The families say that the passage of time and subsequent — sometimes conflicting — investigations have failed to answer fundamental questions about what happened to the students, why and where they were ultimately taken and what role federal institutions like the military played in the tragic event.
"Up to this day, we don't really know what happened to our sons," Tlatempa said.
Sheinbaum announced on Friday that her government would be issuing an update on the progress of the ongoing investigation into the disappearances on Monday.

Her administration arrested the former governor of the state of Guerrero in August and charged him with obstruction of justice and forced disappearances. Mexican authorities are also seeking the extradition of two suspects from the United States, including a former judge who obtained political asylum.
43 Mexican students went missing 12 years ago. Their families want answers
Unravelling 'historical truth'

On Sept. 26, 2014, the students from the Raúl Isidro Burgos Rural Teacher-Training College in Ayotzinapa were in Iguala, Guerrero, to commandeer buses for a rally in Mexico City and take part in a demonstration commemorating the 1968 massacre of university students.

They never arrived. Municipal police officers allegedly attacked the buses, leading to a chaotic night that ended with six deaths — including those of three students — and the disappearance of the 43.

"We are here to demand the return of our 43 comrades alive," Rodrigo, a masked 22-year-old student from the Ayotzinapa college, told CBC News at the protest, adding he would give only his first name due to fear of being targeted by state security forces. "Ayotzinapa won't stop or rest until we find our 43 disappeared comrades."

items: Mexico's top court orders release of 43 missing Ayotzinapa students case file

blocks.text: The administration of Enrique Peña Nieto, who served as president until 2018, initially claimed in its "historical truth" about the events in Iguala that the 43 students had been attacked, taken by municipal police and handed over to a local organized crime group called Guerreros Unidos.

Then-attorney general Jesús Murillo Karam and Tomás Zerón, former head of the criminal investigations agency, claimed the bodies of the students were burned for 14 hours on a pyre at a garbage dump in the municipality of Cocula, which sits about 20 kilometres southwest of Iguala.

Karam, arrested in 2022, is currently under house arrest while facing charges of forced disappearance, torture and obstruction of justice in connection with the handling of the case. Zerón is currently a wanted fugitive reportedly living in Israel.

The term "historical truth" in Mexico is generally used to describe a theory crafted by government players, law enforcement and politicians, often amplified by the media, that becomes the dominant version of a major event.

However, independent international experts disproved the dump cremation theory as scientifically impossible, and a 2018 federal court ruling found that the confessions used by Karam and Zerón to construct their theory were obtained by torture, said lawyer Isidoro Vicario, who represents the families of the 43 missing students.
"The information that was offered has no credibility," he said.

items: Mexican officials make 1st high-level arrest in notorious 2014 disappearance of 43 students

blocks.text: The DNA of three students has so far been matched with remains found in two locations — one found in a river roughly 10 to 12 kilometres downstream from the dump and the two others found in a ravine about 800 metres from the dump.

In March, a Mexican federal court ruled the military needed to release more than 853 pages of information created by its internal intelligence agency that were related to the case. The military had initially denied the existence of the documents.
"To this date [the military] has not complied," Vicario said. "That's also part of what upsets the mothers and fathers."
Expert report connects military to events

A group of experts — created in November 2014 under an agreement between Peña Nieto's government, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and the families — released a report in 2022 that found the military's fingerprints all over the events of Sept. 26, 2014, and in the construction of the discredited theory initially presented by the federal government.
The report, by the Interdisciplinary Group of Independent Experts, found that the Mexican military had both the Ayotzinapa students and the Guerreros Unidos under surveillance.

It also said the military had infiltrated the teachers' college for about a decade and knew the Guerreros Unidos moved heroin to the U.S. using the same types of passenger buses the students had commandeered.

items: Mothers crossing the Mexico-U.S. border risk everything to reunite with their children
Family wants killing of young engineer linked with case of kidnapped Canadian mining firm workers

blocks.text: The report found the local military battalion had real-time surveillance — through cameras and wiretaps — of the violence that unfolded that night in Iguala and that military assets were also stationed near the scene of the conflict.
The report alleged the military was involved in the tortured confessions and that its personnel were also present at the Cocula dump before it was presented as a cremation site.
Mexico’s National Human Rights Commission released a report in July that was widely interpreted as absolving the military of responsibility in the events.

Mediante la #Recomendación 208VG/2026, acreditamos violaciones graves a los derechos humanos de 92 estudiantes de la Escuela Normal Rural “Raúl Isidro Burgos” de Ayotzinapa, así como deficiencias en las investigaciones relacionadas con los hechos ocurridos en Iguala, Guerrero, en… pic.twitter.com/smlzBhJZ3v—CNDH
The families of the 43 met with Supreme Court Chief Justice Hugo Aguilar Ortiz on Friday and discussed the military’s continued non-compliance with the March federal court order to release documents.
"He said he would be reviewing that order that the military provide that information," said Meliton Ortega, whose nephew, Mauricio Ortega Valerio, was 18 when he vanished.
"That information is not going to go directly into the hands of the parents but to the institutions that are still handling the case."

Vicario, the families' lawyer, said the parents also raised the recent referral of the 2018 federal court ruling by Sheinbaum's office to the Supreme Court for review. That decision — which found the Peña Nieto government used torture to obtain confessions — was initially criticized for judicial overreach.

The 2018 ruling called for the creation of a commission of investigation to look into the Ayotzinapa case composed of the head of the National Human Rights Commission, representatives of the parents and the federal attorney general’s office, Vicario said.

"That ruling helped toss the theory of the garbage dump in Cocula. But if the Supreme Court reverses that ruling ... it's a serious problem. It's definitely very risky for the Ayotzinapa case," he said.
'We have to find them'
Time is also an enemy of the families of the 43 young men in their years-long quest for answers. Many of the parents are ailing, and some have died without ever knowing the fate of their sons.
Lourdes Caballero Sanchez's brother, Israel Caballero Sanchez, was 21 when he vanished on the night of Sept. 26, leaving behind an infant daughter.
She said their father died in August 2014 — a month before the tragedy — and their mother passed away last December.
"She left us without knowing about her son," Caballero Sanchez said.

"But I told her, 'Mom, I am here.... Israel still has a family.' His mother, his father are no longer here, but his family still is, and we are going to continue the struggle, for him and for his friends. We have to find them. We have to know where they are, we have to find that truth that we've searched for over the past 12 years."

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial: Lacson remarks on 'too technical' defense strategy
articles.summary: Sen. Panfilo Lacson remarked that the defense seemed to be focusing on too "technical" or minute details, with the result being that much of it is not registering.

blocks.text: Published September 28, 2026 9:06pm

Senator Panfilo Lacson on Monday remarked that the defense seemed to be focusing on too "technical" or minute details, perhaps in a bid to make it appear that proof beyond a reasonable doubt is required, but with the result being that much of it is not registering.

“The way probably and probably some of the non-lawyers among the senator judges, particularly my seatmate, Senator [Lito] Lapid, understand the questions posited by the defense counsel is that the objective of the cross[-examination] was to create an iota of doubt, no matter how technical and small, to create impression that the threshold of establishing guilt is beyond reasonable doubt , which I believe, is not the case in this impeachment trial,” Lacson said.
He was referring to the proof beyond reasonable doubt that is required for conviction in a criminal case, which is different from the requirements for conviction in an impeachment case.
Lacson made the manifestation after defense counsel Robert Narvasa’s cross-examination of Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS) Division Chief Rendell Sopeña.
Sopeña is a witness for Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment, which accuses the Vice President of accumulating unexplained wealth through the following:

items: failure to fully and truthfully disclose all her and her spouse's assets, liabilities, and net worth in her statement of assets, liabilities, and net worth (SALN) including in her SALN for the years 2022, 2023, and 2024; and
failure to divest, and instead, willfully continued, all her business interests during her tenure as vice president for the years 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025.

blocks.text: Narvasa asked the PhilGeps official about the bidding process, questions which were consistently objected to by House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro of Batangas since the PhilGeps is a repository of government contracts and has no mandate to oversee bidding processes.

“Let me clarify, na hindi po ito pre-judgment. Ang hangad ko lang po is baka pwede mag-adjust kayo ng inyong defense strategy kasi I can speak for myself, pagdating sa masyadong technical at ‘yung impression na nagsisilip lang ng napakaliit na butas, mukhang hindi po nag-reregister,” Lacson said.

(Let me clarify that this is not pre-judgment, My goal is that maybe you can adjust your defense strategy because when it comes to too technical issues, and the impression of just nitpicking, it doesn’t quite register.)

“A lot of good points have been raised in this trial. But we are talking among ourselves. Our observation is that parang pong hindi masyadong [nag]re-register, para bang napakaliit na butas na masyadong technical. Medyo hindi po tumatalab,” Lacson added.
(Our observation is, it’s concerns a molehill, if not too technical. It doesn’t make a dent.) — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Schools forced to shut amid burst Thames Water pipe ‘leaking 750 litres a second’
articles.summary:
Leak causes outages and low pressure in parts of London and Surrey, affecting 6,000 properties and leaving some without water

Schools, businesses and homes across seven boroughs in England…

blocks.text: Schools, businesses and homes across seven boroughs in England were hit by a Thames Water outage on Monday, from a burst water main reportedly leaking 750 litres a second.
About 6,000 properties across five south London boroughs and two Surrey boroughs had no water supply or low pressure, Thames Water said.
Thames Water apologised for the lack of water. A spokesperson said: “Our specialist team is now on site and working to stop the water flooding from the broken pipe.”

Schools and colleges were forced to close across the boroughs. Esher College, a sixth form college for 2,000 students, was among those forced to send pupils home and shut their doors. The college said: “Due to a major water outage effecting the KT10 area and our campus we are closed on Monday 28 September.”
Kingston grammar school also closed, as did Long Ditton infant and nursery school, Thames Ditton infant school and Hollyfield school and sixth form centre in Surbiton.

Monica Harding, the Lib Dem MP for Esher and Walton, Surrey, said it was her understanding that water was leaking at 750 litres a second early on Monday morning after a large main burst. The community was left without water from around 5am. “It is completely unacceptable,” she said.
“We need an urgent response from Thames Water to get water supplies back on as soon as possible and to protect vulnerable communities.”
Some reports said a contractor had struck the water pipe with a digger, causing a 4ft rupture in the pipe in the Walton section.
Helen Ryder, who runs a flower shop in Thames Ditton, said: “Our priority is to make sure staff have water, but we need to make sure the flowers do too.
“Hopefully we have enough water, but people come before flowers.”

Parents at Hollyfield school and sixth form centre received a message from the school which said: “There is a significant issue with water supply in the local area … Whilst we have water at the moment it is not replenishing at the same rate it is being used and so our supply will run out at lunchtime. This means that it is unsafe for students to remain on site.”
Thames Water said it would deliver water to registered vulnerable customers and open bottled water stations later, at locations yet to be confirmed.
Thames Water said the following postcodes could be affected: CR4, KT1, KT10, KT12, KT2, KT3, KT5, KT6, KT7, KT8, SM4, SW16, SW17, SW18, SW19, SW20, TW10, TW16.

Paul Kohler, the LibDem MP for Wimbledon said he had contacted Thames Water for more information after reports of a water outage across Wimbledon, New Malden, Raynes Park and Morden, in south London. He told followers on X that he would share any updates he received.
Harding said: “My worry is that decades of underinvestment in our infrastructure and poor regulation may be causing incidences like this.
“Right now, however, the priority must be getting water back in our taps.”
A spokesperson for Thames Water said: “Our engineers are making progress on repairing the burst in Molesey but it is likely to take some time to complete.

“We are rerouting water in the area to reduce the impact on customers while we work to fix the burst. Water deliveries are being made to customers who are on our priority services register. We will be opening bottled water stations this afternoon and will provide their locations once confirmed.

“The number of properties affected has now been reduced to less than 6,000. We again would like to say sorry to our customers and reassure those who are still affected that we are working to restore their water supply as quickly as possible.
“The latest updates will be posted on our website, thameswater.co.uk.”

articles.title: US sanctions on Iran's aviation industry make travel less predictable as countries cancel flights
articles.summary: The threat of secondary US sanctions is putting pressure on airports, fuel suppliers and aviation companies that service Iranian airlines. Some countries have already canceled flights.

image.caption: Mahan Air has been accused of supporting the IRGC [FILE: JUNE 2022]Image: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: US sanctions are pushing Iran's weakened aviation sector toward deeper isolation, making international travel less predictable and raising new risks for trade and cargo.

Earlier in September as part of "operation economic outcast," the US Treasury Department targeted Iran's aviation sector, including Iranian airlines and companies providing ground handling, ticketing or airport support, which face secondary sanctions and potentially lose access to the US financial system.

The United States cannot directly order foreign airports to reject Iranian aircraft. But the threat of secondary sanctions can make servicing them too risky for airports, fuel suppliers and aviation companies.
For Tehran, the aviation sanctions are another layer of Washington's broader pressure campaign, alongside restrictions on banking, shipping, insurance and trade.
Washington argues that Iranian airlines have served not only civilian passengers but also military and security networks.
For example, Mahan Air has been accused of supporting the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and helping transport personnel and equipment.

The issue has also been debated inside Iran. Former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif said in a 2021 interview that Qassem Soleimani had used civilian aircraft to move forces and equipment to Syria.
For Washington, such links help justify targeting aviation networks. For ordinary travelers, however, the immediate result is canceled flights and fewer ways to leave or return to the country.
Major Middle East routes canceled

Iranian flights to Baghdad and Muscat have been suspended or canceled, while Azerbaijan and Georgia also stopped accepting flights operated by Iranian carriers. An Iranian travel agency told DW anonymously for safety reasons that routes to Oman, Iraq, Azerbaijan and Georgia have been seriously disrupted.
On September 24, Turkmenistan refused permission for an Iranian aircraft flying from Tehran to Dushanbe to cross its airspace, forcing the plane to return to Iran.

Turkey, Armenia and China have not announced blanket restrictions, the agency said, but passengers were increasingly reluctant to buy tickets because even a confirmed booking did not guarantee departure.
Is Iran set to become an economic outcast?
A passenger told DW that agencies would still sell him a ticket but could not guarantee the flight would actually operate.

As part of the sanctions package, the US also suspended the "J-1" general license, which had allowed certain non-Iranian aircraft to make temporary stops in Iran under specific conditions, including that control of the aircraft remained with the foreign operator and that the stay did not exceed permitted limits.
Many commercial aircraft contain US-made parts or technology, meaning operations involving Iran can fall under US sanctions rules.

The suspension of J-1 has increased the legal and financial risks for airlines, airports, fuel suppliers, ground-handling companies and other service providers, who now must calculate the risk of secondary sanctions.
More travelers use land crossings
With air connections increasingly uncertain, more passengers are turning to land crossings.
One traveler whose flight was canceled told DW that he traveled overland from Iran to Turkey before continuing to Istanbul by air.
"The border was very crowded. A lot of people were trying to leave because they were worried the routes might close," he told DW anonymously.

For families, elderly passengers, students and patients, however, crossing a land border and continuing by road and air can be far more difficult than taking a direct flight. Costs also rise quickly as passengers add road transport, accommodation and additional flights to journeys that previously required a single ticket.
Also affected is air freight, which is important for urgent or sensitive goods, including some medicines, medical equipment, industrial parts and laboratory samples.
That has become more significant as Iran simultaneously faces severe restrictions on maritime trade.
Iran's shaky aviation industry
Iranian aviation already faced structural problems before the latest sanctions.
Transport Minister Farzaneh Sadegh previously acknowledged that some flights operate without radar guidance, leaving pilots with greater responsibility for navigation.
An ageing fleet, difficulties obtaining spare parts, years of sanctions and fewer operational aircraft have all put pressure on airlines.
When passengers must also consider destination airports refusing services, lengthy delays or flights being canceled without warning, buying a ticket becomes a calculation of risk.

Alireza Salavati, political economy analyst and managing director of the London-based Middle East Analytica, said that the loss of air links will be unlikely to cause a large, immediate hit to Iran's GDP.

"Iran's aviation sector is small by regional standards. Unlike Turkey or the UAE, the country is not a major international hub, and its commercial fleet is limited. Officials said in July that roughly 150 aircraft were in the operational pool, with only about half of them operational at any given time," Salavati told DW.

"The damage is more apparent in connectivity. For a heavily sanctioned economy, flights still matter for business, the diaspora, students, specialist workers and medical treatment abroad. For patients, a once-direct journey can become a detour through a third country, with extra travel, accommodation and sometimes visa costs. Time can matter as much as money," Salavati added.
Iran offers plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz within 7 days
Iran isolated by air and sea
Foreign airlines had already sharply reduced services to Iran before the latest measures.
Many passengers relied on Iranian carriers to reach regional hubs such as Istanbul, Muscat, Baghdad or Yerevan, then continued with foreign airlines.
If those first connections disappear, Iran's international aviation network could increasingly be reduced to a handful of routes that remain politically and commercially viable.

The development also comes as Iran faces restrictions at sea. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, higher insurance and freight costs and pressure on southern ports had already made imports and exports more difficult.
If maritime trade becomes more expensive while air links also contract, Iran will become increasingly dependent on land borders and indirect routes through neighboring states.
Can Iran survive Trump's new sanctions?

articles.title: US response to UN pandemic talks ‘severely weakens’ global planning, says leading health expert
articles.summary:
The US says it is unable to support a major global text on pandemic prevention and preparedness put forward at UN general assembly

The United States government’s decision to block a major…

blocks.text: The United States government’s decision to block a major global declaration on pandemic preparedness “severely weakens” the effort, and signals intent to disrupt international cooperation, says Prof Lawrence Gostin, a leading expert on global health law from Georgetown University.
The United Nations general assembly had been due to adopt a political declaration on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response on 25 September after a high-level meeting on the subject.
The document would have seen countries agree to work together in solidarity to tackle global health threats and express concerns that the world remains unready to deal with future pandemics.

However, the US delegate said it was “not in a position” to support the text, blocking its adoption by consensus – the UN process whereby negotiated documents are assumed to be agreed unless there is an objection.

Italy also rejected the document, while the EU delegate said that although it was “fully and unreservedly committed to the important overarching objective”, there were “red lines” around some references to intellectual property, such as whether the transfer of technology between countries should be voluntary or mandated – a key sticking point in the ongoing World Health Organization treaty negotiations.

Dr Erica Schwartz, the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said critical issues remained unresolved, referring to “the inclusion of divisive ideologies that lack definitional consensus” and references within the document to ongoing, WHO-led negotiations over the fair sharing of vaccines and drugs between countries in any future pandemic.

blocks.caption: Erica Schwartz, director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: It is understood that the Trump administration was unhappy with mentions of equity and universal access to sexual and reproductive healthcare services. Earlier this year, President Trump signed executive orders expanding a “global gag” rule that bans US aid recipients from work related to abortion to also include bans on diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives and what it called “gender ideology”.

A separate WHO-led agreement governing how the world should respond to future pandemics is on hold while countries try to find agreement on the issue of pathogen access and benefit sharing – or what countries should be guaranteed in terms of vaccines and treatments in return for sharing data on any emerging diseases on their territory. The US withdrew from the WHO shortly after Trump took office.
UN documents of this kind do not impose legally binding requirements on countries but instead serve as a sign of commitment and intent.
Gostin said: “Since this is a political declaration, its value is only as strong as the political will to adopt and implement its provisions. The US decision to dissent severely weakens the document.

“For many decades, it was American financing and scientific innovations that were the bedrock of outbreak detection and response. This signals a clear US intention not to cooperate globally to health threats common to all nations. There is no rational reason to reject a political commitment to preventing and responding to dangerous outbreaks. The only thing gained by the Trump administration is to put a stick in the wheels of international cooperation.”
The US has been accused of exploitation in its pursuit of individual agreements with poorer countries in return for aid.
​The political declaration ​i​s still likely to be ​adopted when it is considered again ​at a later UN general assembly meeting​ where a majority rather than consensus vote is needed.

Helen Clark, a former prime minister of New Zealand and a co-chair of the Independent Panel for Pandemic Preparedness and Response, said: “It is disappointing that the high level meeting was not asked to endorse the political declaration which had been negotiated by member states. Agreeing to collaborate to prevent, prepare for and respond to pandemics should not be controversial.”

Eloise Todd, the executive director and founder of Resilience Action Network International, said: “It is unacceptable that member states were unable to advance a political declaration at the close of the high level meeting on Friday, and an unfortunate reminder of the continued challenges to drive consensus for the global good in the current geopolitical environment.”

articles.title: Plan for controversial Sydney data centre scrapped after push-back
articles.summary: Goodman Group, the property giant behind the Project Mars data centre, says the decision is due to changes to the "policy and regulatory environment".

blocks.text: Plans for a data centre which would have been built metres from people's homes in a Sydney suburb have been scrapped following intense push-back by campaigners.

The data centre was being developed by Goodman Group, Australia's biggest property company, and would have seen it construct a A$1.2bn (£630m; $841m), 90-megawatt facility known as Project Mars in the Lane Cove area.
The company confirmed it was withdrawing its application in a letter to the local planning authority. It follows a concerted opposition against the data centre by local residents and campaigners.
The dispute captures a wider disagreement in Australia over the role of data centres.

With the mainstreaming of generative AI in recent years, there has been a huge swell in demand for data centres, and Australia - with its abundance of clean energy, natural gas reserves, and land - has become a global destination for their construction.

However, while the country's government has been keen to attract investment from global AI companies, there has also been stiff opposition due to the huge demands the centres place on water and energy supplies, and the disruption they cause local communities.

The proposal for Project Mars, which would have been constructed about 20 metres from the nearest house in the suburb of Lane Cove, received 374 submissions during a consultation - with just nine in support of it.
According to local news website In the Cove, this is highest number of submissions ever received for a data centre application, external.

In its letter to New South Wales Department of Planning, Goodman Group said since starting the planning process in March 2025, it had "undertaken extensive technical investigations, stakeholder engagement and community consultation".
"During this time, the policy and regulatory environment for large-scale data centre development has evolved significantly," it said.
It said it had "carefully considered these changes" along with the "views of the local community", and concluded it would not proceed with the development.
The decision by Goodman Group follows an announcement by the New South Wales government last month that it would be introducing a fast-track programme for data centres.
The programme would allow them to be assessed within 75 days, provided they meet requirements around certain standards and fund the additional supply of water and energy.

In a message posted to the Facebook page of Lane Cove Responsible Planning Group, Anthony Roberts, a member of the New South Wales Legislative Assembly representing Lane Cove, said it was "a huge win for the Lane Cove West community".
"This is a common-sense win for our community," he said.
"This victory sends a clear message to other data centre developers. To find suitable locations before putting proposals forward.
"Data centres have an important role to play, but developments of this size and scale need to be appropriately located and planned with the surrounding community in mind."

articles.title: COA flags ghost, incomplete school projects in Davao del Norte
articles.summary: In Talaingod, Davao del Norte, state auditors flag a ghost school building at Kamingawan Elementary School, and undelivered project inclusions at Dulyan Integrated School

blocks.text: In Talaingod, Davao del Norte, state auditors flag a ghost school building at Kamingawan Elementary School, and undelivered project inclusions at Dulyan Integrated School

MANILA, Philippines – Around P83.26 million worth of school infrastructure projects in Davao del Norte were flagged by the Commission on Audit (COA) as ghost or non-existent, as well as “abandoned and materially incomplete” even though payments were nearly completed.
In its 2025 annual audit report on the Department of Education (DepEd), COA said the infrastructure work for Kamingawan Elementary School in Talaingod town was a “ghost/non-existent project.”
“No structure was found upon inspection but paid up to 98.8%,” state auditors noted in the report released last Wednesday, September 23.
The project was for the construction of a one-storey, two-classroom school building with a solar photovoltaic (PV) system, school furniture, and rainwater collector and water system.
A similar project for Dulyan Integrated School in Talaingod was also flagged by COA.

State auditors said that while the building and the rainwater system were constructed at Dulyan Integrated School, the “solar PV energy system as well as school furniture were not delivered,” but it was already “paid up to 98.80%.”
Both school projects were covered by a contract amounting to P36.36 million under the DepEd’s Last Mile Schools Program (LMSP), according to COA.
The commission also found another problematic LMSP project at Dugayan National High School in Kapalong town.

It had a P25.61-million contract for a two-storey, six-classroom school building with a toilet, rainwater collector, school furniture, solar PV energy system, and water system. It was already paid up to 98.90%.
“Upon inspection, building construction was found to be largely incomplete and abandoned. Only the structural frame had been constructed,” state auditors said.

COA also reported that distribution transformers, multiple panel boards, and outlets “remain uninstalled and undelivered” for New Casay Integrated School in Braulio E. Dujali town and Carmen National High School in Carmen town. Roofing works at Carmen National High School were also not performed.
The flagged school electrification projects were worth P10.43 million.

Moreover, state auditors found that four classrooms at Datu Balong National High School in San Isidro town were “unrepaired but claimed as implemented and paid up to 98.18% on July 18, 2025.” The contract was worth P7.54 million.
They also said that the construction of health facilities at Gov. Dujali Elementary School in San Isidro was “largely incomplete and abandoned.” It had a price tag of P3.32 million.
COA recommended the issuance of notices of termination of all contracts for the flagged projects, and to initiate blacklisting proceedings against the erring contractors.

State auditors told the Davao del Norte Schools Division Office (SDO) to conduct a fact-finding investigation to determine the accountability of concerned officials, initiate recovery proceedings for all paid progress billings, and file appropriate administrative, criminal, and civil charges against responsible officers and private individuals.
They also told the Davao del Norte SDO to immediately conduct joint validation of completely delivered items to correct accounting records.
State auditors also flagged deficiencies in monitoring the implementation of the DepEd’s Senior High School (SHS) Voucher Program.

In particular, guidelines for the complete monitoring and validation procedures for the SHS Voucher Program in the Ilocos Region were “not consistently followed,” which undermined the reliability of monitoring results during the audit period.
According to COA, the DepEd regional office took corrective steps from August 18 to 26.

“While the measures appear responsive to the identified deficiencies, their actual implementation and impact on ensuring compliance, detecting program violations, and validating the existence and eligibility of beneficiaries remain to be established,” state auditors said in a rejoinder.

They requested the DepEd office in the Ilocos Region to submit the comprehensive results of the 100% on-site monitoring activities, including detailed documentation of validation procedures, discrepancies, and corrective actions.

The regional office was also told to use a uniform monitoring and compliance report template to “ensure consistent verification of the existence, eligibility, and completeness of records of all SHS [Voucher Program] beneficiaries, and to enhance detection of program violations, including ghost students.”
Meanwhile, there were “inadequate payment controls” in six DepEd regional offices, which “[increased] the risk of overpayment, ghost employees, and erroneous salary payments.”
The deficiencies found were in the established payroll systems, as well as preparation, processing, and payment of salaries.
The DepEd regional offices identified in the audit observations were in the National Capital Region, Ilocos Region, Cagayan Valley, Central Luzon, Calabarzon, and Davao Region. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Healey vows to stick to fiscal rules in budget built on hope
articles.summary: Chancellor tells Labour conference it’s ‘not progressive’ to fail to balance books amid rising welfare bill as borrowing costs climb to record high

blocks.text: John Healey has pledged to use next month’s budget to inject hope into Britain’s economy while sticking to the government’s fiscal rules, arguing there is “nothing progressive” about losing control of public finances.
In his first speech as chancellor to Labour conference, Healey warned that next month’s highly anticipated tax-and-spending event would need to take into account a challenging global backdrop.

Setting out measures to support jobs and growth, the chancellor announced a new local apprenticeship service, led by mayors, targeted at young people to deliver “thousands more apprenticeships” across the country.

He also signalled Labour was gearing up for welfare reform designed to tackle a sharp rise in youth unemployment, saying that it “falls to us to act” to overhaul the benefits system and it is “simply not progressive to allow a bigger and bigger benefits bill”.

Insisting he would balance the books while fleshing out Andy Burnham’s plans to strengthen “growth in every postcode”, Healey said he and the prime minister were in “lockstep” in their commitment to balance the books.
“That commitment is so important. There is nothing progressive about losing control because it’s always working people who pay for it,” he said.
Against a backdrop of jitters in financial markets as the Iran war rattles the global economy, the UK government’s borrowing costs have risen to the highest levels for almost two decades.
Economists have warned that the chancellor could be forced to increase taxes or cut spending in response to rising spending pressures, and the economic fallout ripples through global bond markets.

In a speech aiming to strike a balance between promising to fund the new prime minister’s priorities while committing to fiscal discipline, Healey drew a comparison with the 1990s when he was an adviser to Gordon Brown.

Wearing a red tie that he had lent to the then chancellor to wear for a Labour conference speech in Bournemouth more than two decades ago, he said the money New Labour had in the 1990s “is simply not there now”.

Teeing up a tough budget, in which Burnham has warned “difficult decisions” will need to be taken, Healey said the government needed to hold firm in its main fiscal rule requiring day-to-day spending to be matched by revenues by 2030.
He also sought to draw a distinction between Labour’s approach and that of the Conservatives, saying Britain was suffering from the “reckless actions” the party had taken since 2010.
after newsletter promotion

“Britain has it harder now. We had 13 years of flatlining tory growth in living standards when Cameron’s austerity gutted our public services, when Johnson’s Brexit hammered our exports and Truss’s mini budget crashed our economy,” he said.

He also accused Reform of taking a reckless approach to the public finances while prioritising the interests of “dodgy” billionaire donors, saying that Nigel Farage was “Liz Truss with a bitcoin account.”

Healey’s local apprenticeships announcement comes as ministers await recommendations from a highly anticipated report by Alan Milburn, the former Labour cabinet minister, who is leading a review into Britain’s crisis in youth worklessness.
The chancellor also said he wanted to usher in a “new age of industrialisation,” announcing £6bn of contracts for our British shipyards

Using Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool to spell out his agenda for government, Burnham has pledged to “rip the plaster off” to fix Britain’s social care system and announced a new help-to-buy scheme to support young people to get on the housing ladder.

articles.title: Nor’easter storm floods coastal areas from New Jersey to New England
articles.summary:
Powerful weather system pummels shoreline for a second day, knocking out power to tens of thousands

Residents of coastal communities in the US’s north-east slogged through floodwaters for a…

blocks.text: Residents of coastal communities in the US’s north-east slogged through floodwaters for a second day as a powerful storm known as a nor’easter pummeled the shoreline on Sunday, knocking out power to tens of thousands of homes.
Tidal surges swamped low-lying neighborhoods in New Jersey while wind gusts toppled trees on New York’s Long Island, damaging homes and bringing down utility poles.

In the New Jersey beach town of Sea Bright, each high tide brought a new round of flooding. “It’s not like a one-time occurrence,” said Caroline Virenius, whose garage filled with about a foot of water (30cm). “It’s getting wet again and again.”

The slow-moving storm, which killed a New York City Housing Authority worker when a tree fell on Saturday, was expected to linger through Sunday with heavy rain, strong winds and dangerous surf all the way to New England.

Extreme amounts of rain – more than 4 inches (10cm) since Friday in some spots in New Jersey – combined with a surging ocean led to flooding amounts not seen for close to a decade in places used to dealing with high water, residents said.

The National Weather Service (NWS) predicted the storm would weaken over Sunday night with local heavy rain in parts of New England and the mid-Atlantic. But local officials in New Jersey and New York told residents that high tide late on Monday could bring more flooding.
“There is another band of the storm, a weaker band, but still another band that could hit early this afternoon and later into the evening,” said New York’s Nassau county executive, Bruce Blakeman.

The nor’easter triggered memories of Superstorm Sandy, which left behind over $60bn in damage across the eastern US in 2012. While this storm’s impact has been nowhere near that, it could be the first of several along the east coast during the fall because of an El Niño climate pattern that is disrupting this year’s weather.
Images of waves crashing into sea walls and on to beaches raised concerns about coastal erosion.

Well over 100,000 customers were without power across the north-east and mid-Atlantic at times on Sunday, according to PowerOutage.us. The most widespread outages were in counties along the coast from New Jersey to Connecticut.

The total number of outages across the US had fallen on Monday morning to about 55,000, with more than 10,000 of those reported in Hawaii, which was dealing with the threat of heavy, flash flooding and strong winds as Hurricane Nolo moved away from the state.

Numerous flights were canceled or delayed up and down the east coast. More than 250 flights had been canceled at Boston Logan international airport by late Sunday morning as wind gusts reached 40mph (64km/h), according to the Massachusetts Port Authority.
The worst of the remaining rainfall was expected on Sunday from northern New Jersey into southern New England.

While the storm was gradually weakening, tidal flooding would stay through high-tide cycles on Sunday night, said Bob Oravec, a lead forecaster with the National Weather Service (NWS) in College Park, Maryland.
In New York City, water a few inches deep filled streets in the Howard Beach neighborhood but did not deter residents from venturing out for coffee on Sunday morning.
Carole Ann Palmer, who owns Jingles Bait and Tackle in North Beach Haven, New Jersey, said this was the worst flooding she had seen in 10 years.
“Yesterday, I was like, oh my God, it just keeps getting higher and higher,” said Palmer, who lives above the store.
The front step was swept away in the storm, and she saw neighbors kayaking through the streets on Saturday.
Her biggest problem on Sunday was taking her two puppies outside to relieve themselves. She had to put on waders and carry them to dry land.
“I take one at the time, carry them across the street so they can do their business and then come back, dry them off and then do the other one. It’s a workout,” Palmer said.
Bernard Dowd waded through tidal water on Sunday to get to his Sea Bright home, a day after he got back from work to find his basement “filled up like a swimming pool”.

But he said the situation around his neighborhood would probably have been much worse if it were not for new rules requiring homeowners to raise the height of their homes in the wake of Sandy, which devastated the community.
He also noticed that many around the community had lined their homes and businesses with sandbags – something he wishes he had done too.
“I’m always thinking they are hyping the storm,” he said.

articles.title: The Mighty Sparrow, Caribbean music legend, dead at 91
articles.summary: The Mighty Sparrow, the Grenada-born, Trinidadian-raised musician who helped export calypso to the masses beginning in the 1950s, has died. He was 91.

image.caption: The Mighty Sparrow accepts an award during the Bollywood Music Awards in Atlantic City, N.J., on Nov. 4, 2006. (Tim Shaffer/Reuters)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
The Mighty Sparrow, the Grenada-born, Trinidadian-raised musician who helped export calypso to the masses beginning in the 1950s, has died. He was 91.
'His songs became part of the soundtrack of Caribbean life and culture': Jamaican PM
The Mighty Sparrow, who helped export calypso music to the masses beginning in the 1950s, has died. He was 91.

Born Slinger Francisco, he died peacefully surrounded by his family in New York, his family said in a statement. His death came after a "brief illness," the statement said, without disclosing any other details.
"He was an institution in the entertainment industry, well admired for his skill and finesse as a singer, songwriter and mentor; beloved by many," Francisco's family said.
Born in the coastal town of Grand Roy, Grenada, in July 1935, Francisco was just a toddler when he migrated with his parents to Trinidad and Tobago in 1937.

Trinidad and Tobago is the birthplace of calypso music, and it's where the name and persona of the Mighty Sparrow would emerge to produce a list of hit songs in the genre: Jean and Dinah, Both of Them, Congo Man, Mr. Walker, The Lizard and many more.

"Through his music, his wit and his unmatched contribution to culture, he carried the spirit and stories of our people across the world," said Kamla Persad Bissessar, the country's prime minister. "For decades, Sparrow has been part of the soundtrack of Trinidad and Tobago. His music made us laugh, made us think and made us proud of who we are."
Wide-ranging songs
Trinidad and Tobago has honoured the composer and performer with national awards, and in 1987, the University of the West Indies conferred an honorary Doctor of Letters on Francisco.

"A titan has transitioned, a legend has left," the consulate general for Trinidad and Tobago in Toronto said in a social media post. "Thank you for sharing your genius with us and leaving us with a legacy that will stand every test of time."
The performer's stature was reflected by the fact that leaders of Jamaica, Barbados and Dominica, among others, took time on Sunday to pay tribute.

"His songs became part of the soundtrack of Caribbean life and culture, beloved by generations of Jamaicans and people across the region," said Jamaican Prime Minister Andrew Holness. "I extend my condolences to his family, the people of Trinidad and Tobago, and the people of Grenada, where he was born."

Francisco recorded hundreds of songs in a career that spanned six decades. He performed in several countries around the world, including at famous venues such as New York City's Madison Square Garden.

GOODBYE TO THE GREATEST Today, our nation mourns the loss of an icon whose legacy will forever live in the hearts of all citizens of Trinidad and Tobago. Sparrow was a true patriot and revered ambassador of Trinidad and Tobago’s culture. Through his music, his wit and his unmatched contribution to culture, he carried the spirit and stories of our people across the world. For decades, Sparrow has been part of the soundtrack of Trinidad and Tobago. His music made us laugh, made us think and made us proud of who we are. On behalf of the Government and people of Trinidad and Tobago, I extend my deepest condolences to his family and loved ones. Rest in peace, Mighty Sparrow. Your voice will live on forever. 🇹🇹🕊️—PM_Kamla

While the Mighty Sparrow carried on the party tradition of a genre popularized through the Caribbean's carnival culture, other songs were topical and even political. They included Model Nation, celebrating Trinidad and Tobago's independence in 1962, Martin Luther King For President, and Kennedy and Kruschev, referencing the American and Soviet leaders during the height of the Cold War.
The singer also celebrated Toronto's burgeoning Caribana festival in 1972 with Toronto Mas.

He returned to the city many times, including in 2014 for the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) screening of the documentary The Glamour Boyz Again: The Mighty Sparrow and Lord Superior on the Hilton Rooftop. He had survived a diabetic coma the previous year.
Writing in 2021 on five pieces of music that influenced him, Canadian conductor and CBC Centrestage host Daniel Bartholomew-Poyser included the calypso artist's Jean and Dinah.

"In this song, Mighty Sparrow deals with, among other things, the economic impact of the closure of American military bases in Trinidad. But you might be too busy dancing to notice," said Bartholomew-Poyser.
"I am grateful this music informed my childhood," said the conductor, born to Trinidadian and Jamaican parents.

items: The King of Soca went back school to learn more about his craft
Harry Belafonte, legendary performer and activist, dead at 96

blocks.text: Throughout his career, Francisco's goal was to advance the calypso art form, according to Trinidadian cultural historian and author Rudolph Ottley.
"The Mighty Sparrow was the supreme entertainer, a cultural revolutionary and one of the world's greatest calypsonians," Ottley told The Associated Press.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Chris Iorfida, based in Toronto, has been with CBC since 2002 and written on subjects as diverse as politics, business, health, sports, arts and entertainment, science and technology.
With files from the Associated Press

articles.title: Decades of fossil fuel influence paved way for Trump’s assault on university research, study says
articles.summary:
Fossil fuel firms have spent years trying to regulate climate research by donating to US universities, study authors argue

Recent attacks on US universities by the Trump administration have…

blocks.text: Recent attacks on US universities by the Trump administration have built on decades of efforts by libertarian donor networks, fossil fuel companies and conservative thinktanks to reshape university governance and increase outside influence, according to a new study.
The authors of the new perspective study argue that the erosion of university autonomy has left colleges more vulnerable to corporate interests, especially within climate and energy research.

In 2025, the Trump administration froze billions of dollars in research funding, launched investigations into 75 institutions and pushed colleges to sign agreements supporting administration policies in exchange for federal funding. The federal government canceled $4m in climate research grants at Princeton University alone and accused scientists of fueling “climate anxiety”.

If you’re a young researcher watching that, you might think twice about asking a question that could cost you your funding, said Noel Healy, of Salem State University, the lead author of the study published in the journal Energy Research & Social Science.
“Climate policy is only as good as the evidence behind it. When the industry being regulated gets to shape the questions researchers ask, it ends up shaping the policy too,” he said.

The Academic Freedom Index, which measures how freely scholars and universities can teach, research and express ideas without interference, found that US institutional autonomy fell from 3.3 in 2019 to 1.7 in 2025, on a scale of 0 to 4.

blocks.caption: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) has defended its policies around fossil fuel donations and endowments from fossil fuel companies. Photograph: Erica Denhoff/Icon Sportswire/Getty Images

blocks.text: “Since 2025, scientists have been deleting words like ‘climate change’ from their grant applications because those words can get an application rejected,” Healy said. “Some universities have shut down programs before the government even asked them to, hoping to avoid becoming a target. You don’t have to ban speech if people fear that speaking up will cost them their funding. People start deciding it’s safer to stay quiet.”

Outside influence on US universities is not new. In the 1920s, electric utilities worked with academics to defend their monopoly positions and oppose regulations. Fossil fuel companies followed suit in the 1950s, funding research to sow doubt about the public health impacts of their products. Internal industry documents have shown that companies viewed academic research as a way to build credibility and influence public debate.

Corporate-funded research was only one way powerful interests influenced universities. Libertarian donor networks also influenced program content, faculty hiring and gained appointments to university governing bodies. For example, David Koch, the billionaire industrialist whose wealth came from Koch Industries, gave more than $185m to his alma mater, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), and served as a lifetime member to the elite research university’s highest governing body.

Between 2010 and 2020, six fossil fuel companies alone gave more than $700m to US universities, helping to legitimize industry solutions to the climate crisis and undermine regulatory approaches. Some of this funding came with donor agreements that gave outside actors control over decisions traditionally made by faculty, such as in hiring and curricula.

At the same time, donor-influence models were written into state law. For example, in 2016, the Arizona state legislature created the first publicly funded libertarian academic center. Other states have followed suit. These centers bypass faculty control, instead answering to legislators. These centers are expected to receive $50m in US taxpayer dollars during the 2025-2026 school year, according to reporting by the Hechinger Report.

State legislatures have also tried to limit faculty power through legislation that could abolish tenure, block faculty participation in lawsuits and police educational programming. From 2021 to 2023, more than 150 state bills were introduced targeting tenure, faculty governance, and diversity, equity and inclusion, according to the Energy Research & Social Science perspective.

Soaring tuition and student debt, which are also products of the corporate model, have contributed to mistrust in higher education. The authors of the study argue that to regain public trust, administrators must confront how corporate donors have reshaped their priorities, disclose donor contributions and influence, and give faculty committees the ability to reject funding that undermines the university’s public mission and create conflicts of interest. Union contracts can protect faculty and empower them to confront corporate capture.

“Transparency lets you see the deal, but it doesn’t let you stop it. Faculty need the power to review major gifts before they’re accepted and to refuse the ones that threaten academic freedom,” Healy said.

Universities don’t have to start from scratch. For example, the national UnKoch My Campus campaign published a model gift-acceptance policy that gives faculty a say before gifts with conditions are accepted, makes donor agreements public and sets clear grounds for rejecting gifts that give donors influence over hiring or teaching. Universities can draw on examples like this to write their own rules, Healy said.

“In other countries, attacks on university legitimacy paved the way for faculty purges, campus closures and centralized political control,” he said. “Universities came under attack before those governments had full control, not after.”

MIT has previously said it would not divest its endowment from fossil-fuel companies, arguing that working with industry could help develop climate solutions. The MIT Energy Initiative has also said that funders have no control over the content or findings of its research reports.

articles.title: Teachers at Euan Blair firm report ‘horrendous stress’ after AI used to rate their work
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Instructors at tech training company Multiverse hit out at ‘remorseless’ and ‘unnerving’ monitoring system

Teachers at Euan Blair’s £1.6bn tech training company, Multiverse, have…

blocks.text: Teachers at Euan Blair’s £1.6bn tech training company, Multiverse, have blown the whistle about “horrendous stress” and feeling constantly watched after bosses started using AI models to surveil and rate their teaching.

Staff delivering apprenticeship training in computer and AI skills to thousands of UK public and private sector workers now have transcripts of online classroom sessions analysed and scored by an AI programmed to alert human managers when they are suspected of doing things wrong.

The AI is trained to flag problems in their performance ranging from not fixing a disruption to the online connection quickly enough – within about a minute – to using too many “filler” phrases, such as “sort of” and “kind of”.
Teachers called the newly introduced system “remorseless” and “unnerving”, and said some staff were on edge, losing sleep, and seeking therapy.

Multiverse was co-founded by the eldest son of the former prime minister Tony Blair and employs more than 800 people. It supplies AI and digital skills training to workers in the NHS, local councils, universities and the private sector, mostly funded through the government’s apprenticeship levy.

blocks.caption: Euan Blair owns a large minority stake in Multiverse, putting his personal net worth at an estimated £350m.  Photograph: Yui Mok/PA

blocks.text: Alongside his father, Blair is one of the biggest cheerleaders for wider AI adoption in the UK economy, claiming last week that “every single worker is going to need to be retrained” and that employers want their workforces “as AI-pilled as possible”. Multiverse uses a mix of AI models including Anthropic and OpenAI products.

Its new AI teacher monitoring system tags each instructor by their “risk status”, calculates a “percentage confidence score” and produces written comments about teachers’ work for managers to see at a glance.

It is only the latest example of employers using AI to track worker behaviour. Earlier this year Burger King started using AI to track restaurant workers’ customer interactions and this summer Meta paused tracking of employees’ computer keystrokes amid data privacy concerns and a staff backlash.

With critics warning AI monitoring risks eroding human agency, one study has suggested it can backfire by turning workers rebellious and new research to be published this week reports that workers in the wider UK tech industry are finding AI degrades work satisfaction. The United Tech and Allied Workers branch of the Communication Workers Union concluded AI causes “cognitive surrender” as workers lose skills and confidence and often intensifies rather than eases work.

“Since all of this has come in, the stress level has been absolutely horrendous,” said one of several Multiverse teachers who spoke on condition of anonymity. “It has affected sleep, and not just for me. I’ve gone through a lot of things in my life, and I haven’t ever been in a position where I’m waking up in the middle of the night.”

Previously instructors were observed monthly by a human manager but are now watched for several hours per day by an AI. It is trained to consider marking instructors down if they give vague or uncertain answers to questions, if learners go quiet when asked to contribute and if the teacher gets pulled into a prolonged one-to-one exchange that sidelines the group.

“This is inducing stress because you consistently have to be cautious,” one teacher said. “Your attention is no longer delivering [the lesson] and listening to the learner [but] am I saying the right thing so the AI doesn’t mark me down for something stupid that I’ve mistakenly said.”
Another teacher called it “very uncomfortable”.

Multiverse says the AI does not replace human judgment but “directs human time to where it’s needed most” by highlighting problem. A spokesperson said it was “using AI to improve the experience of learners and customers”, and that only human managers wrote teachers’ performance reviews.

They did not directly address complaints the system caused stress and anxiety and felt “remorseless”, but said its introduction was communicated in advance and teachers will have access to the data the AI collects.

“This agent provides instructors with improved advice on development and feedback – exactly how any learning organisation should be deploying AI,” the spokesperson said. “The most consequential performance management action it can take is to recommend that a human personally reviews a session.”

Blair owns a large minority stake in Multiverse, putting his personal net worth at an estimated £350m. The company was recently valued at £1.6bn albeit on a turnover of £118m and losses of £28m last year. In February, Ofsted, the UK education inspectorate, found Multiverse failed to meet expected standards in several areas, but praised the instructors as “skilled, effective teachers”.

Its new AI monitoring agent, introduced in recent weeks, is trained to spot signs an instructor has not fully internalised the teaching material. The AI is instructed to count verbal tics that point to that conclusion and to “judge the PATTERN across the whole transcript, not isolated instances”.

It says: “1-2 hedges or filler words in an otherwise direct, well-internalised explanation do NOT fail this standard … What fails the standard is a PERVASIVE REPEATED pattern of filler, hedging or re-explanation.”

When a trainer is setting a task “if the instructor is visibly confused themselves or had to self-correct while giving the instruction, that confusion itself counts as evidence the instruction was not clear the first time”. The AI is told to apply a negative mark “even if it was eventually straightened out”.
after newsletter promotion
The workers said the AI monitoring has led to managers pulling them up for suspected “digressions” when in fact they were answering a student’s question.
“It’s impossible for me not to be affected by this mentally,” one teacher said.

“I feel like I’m under continuous scrutiny,” another said. “It’s all about what I didn’t do in this session rather than what I did do. Did I do something incorrectly yesterday? What will I mess up on today? It’s remorseless. I don’t know why this is happening.”

John Chadfield, national tech officer at the CWU, said the public would be horrified to hear of bosses “deploying deeply intrusive surveillance on workers” but said “this news won’t surprise tech workers who feel the reality of the tech sector – an industry in serious need of further regulation.”

He called for new laws to ensure AI is deployed in a socially responsible way and not to “shut off job opportunities for young people, degrade the craft of skilled workers and make astronomical profit for a few”.
Case study: ‘An AI judges my lessons. Multiverse calls it quality assurance – it feels like surveillance’

Being constantly monitored by an AI is deeply uncomfortable. Imagine every word you say on the job being checked against a rubric that dictates what you’re expected to say and how. That’s the reality for me and my colleagues: every session we deliver to apprentices is now recorded and transcribed. It feels intrusive. Multiverse calls it quality assurance, but it feels like surveillance.

Managers can now look at a dashboard showing how the AI has judged each of our sessions. It assigns a risk level to each of us: the risk of not having said the right things. That’s stressful, for several reasons.

First, the AI isn’t always accurate. Managers are now tasked to investigate trainers for not following the script – at least according to the AI – when actually they were adapting the lesson to a learner’s needs. The threat of being questioned in such detail, at any time, is a constant source of anxiety.

Second, there is no transparency. During the rollout, all delivery staff were kept in the dark while the system was developed. We have no insight into the AI’s analysis. The company says staff will get dashboard access in time, but for now only managers can see it.

The need to always be cautious warps your priorities. Instead of focusing attention on the learner, you become obsessed with whether you’re saying the right thing. Being on camera for most of the day is stressful in itself; being haunted by an AI makes it worse.

A more productive way to use AI would be to improve the teaching materials and raise the standard of what we teach. Instead, the AI is checking whether the teacher managed to fill the gaps? As it stands, this is surveillance, not empowerment.

And I’m worried about what this data is for. In a climate of AI replacing people, I can’t help but worry it will be used to train AI to replace coaches and instructors altogether. Apprentices don’t want that and neither do I, and I would never consent to my sessions being used this way.

articles.title: 'Only up from here': Tempo's off-court success offers optimism after injury-ravaged inaugural campaign
articles.summary: The last two months of the season for Toronto’s WNBA franchise was a gruelling, slow-motion march simply trying to navigate an injury-depleted roster. Still, there were memorable on-court highlights…

image.caption: Tempo players applaud fans in Toronto following the team's final home game of its inaugural season. While the franchise fell short of some of its lofty goals in its first campaign, there is reason for optimism going forward. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: It had been a long and trying season for the head coach of the Toronto Tempo and Sandy Brondello looked more exhausted than energized.

One of the WNBA’s premier tacticians with two championships and two additional Finals appearances on her resume, Brondello had never missed the WNBA playoffs as a head coach over 13 seasons prior to this year.

But the post-season had been gone for many months and here she was 10 minutes after a 14-point loss to the woeful Connecticut Sun acutely aware of the reality in front of her — an 11-33 season that included losing 22 of their last 24 games.
The last two months of the season for Toronto’s WNBA franchise was a gruelling, slow-motion march simply trying to navigate an injury-depleted roster.

How bad did it get for the Tempo? The team ranked first overall in the WNBA in games lost to in-season injuries (121 games). You want another telling statistic that encapsulated the year? The quartet of Brittany Sykes, Marina Mabrey, Nyara Sabally, and Kiki Rice — the team’s most talented players— played a total of just 78 minutes together this season. That’s 95 minutes less than the running time of the hit film, The Odyssey.

“I told them after the game about how special it is being the first team in Canada and how our fans still supported us, even though we weren't winning many games,” Brondello said on a folding chair, flanked by Rice and Isabelle Harrison.

“Losing didn't take us away from being the best team that we could be given what we were facing. I don't think any other team in the history of the league had had so many in-season injuries. … Character is shown in face of adversity and I think we handled it as well as we could. But now it's remembering — we don't want to go through this shit again.”

Expansion teams always struggle with depth, which made the injuries to the Tempo’s starters impossible to overcome. The team’s million-dollar backcourt of Sykes (23 games) and Mabrey (eight games) missed 31 games combined. Rice was sidelined for almost all of June and July. The Tempo faded in a ton of games in the final two quarters, as players were clearly gassed.

The brutal truth is their play after the World Cup break was poor. Belgian point guard Julie Allemand said in her exit interview with the media that the team needed to be tougher and better focused on details even through the injuries. She was disappointed in the final four games, as was Brondello.
Memorable moments

Still, there were memorable on-court highlights including the first-ever win on May 13 in its second-ever game, a 7-5 start to the season, and Marina Mabrey’s 53-point outburst in a rout of the Los Angeles Sparks on June 25, tying the WNBA single-game scoring record.
Mabrey was selected to the WNBA All-Star Game the following month, a nice first for the franchise.
Rice, the team’s No. 1 pick, landed on the AP’s All-Rookie Team after averaging 13.4 points with a 47.2 field goal percentage over 28 games.
Marina Mabrey ties WNBA record with 53 points, leads Tempo to dominating win over Sparks
“If you can't embrace hard, you probably shouldn't be in this league,” Brondello said.

“What we do every day, day in, day out, wins or losses, highs and lows, injuries, not injuries, is tough. There were only a few games where I was a little disappointed with our effort. Overall, I think their resiliency, their togetherness has been commendable. That's all you can ask for in a season with so much adversity. There's some things that we can be really excited about as we move forward into 2027.”

Where the franchise really soared was how the community received them. There was an expectation that this season would be a honeymoon for the team no matter the record given how long women’s basketball fans had waited for the WNBA to come to Canada. You saw that for the entire season.

The crowds at Coca-Cola Coliseum and Scotiabank Arena were voracious for the WNBA, including the visiting teams. Every game at Coca-Cola was a sellout and the Tempo set a WNBA regular-season attendance record of 20,996 fans for their first-ever game in Montreal at the Bell Centre on July 10.
Commercial, brand goals achieved

One of the things Tempo management prioritized in 2026 was brand awareness across Canada and the markers indicate big success. According to the team, the Tempo generated 98,000 media stories during the season which they estimated the reach at 346 billion earned media impressions.

Between May 8 and the final game on Sept. 24, they gained nearly 94,000 social media followers across multiple platforms and should soon hit 400,000 social media followers across multiple platforms. ESPN produced a documentary (“Setting The Tempo”) on the making of the team, which was a nice bit of brand exposure in the United States. The media deal with TSN produced games being shown across Canada and the network invested in on-air talent and shoulder programming.

The franchise adeptly navigated the one crisis PR moment of the year when Brondello was suspended for one game by the WNBA for an inappropriate comment she said about Angel Reese during a game against the Atlanta Dream.

“We have done very well at reaching franchise commercial and brand metrics that we had set out to reach,” Tempo president Teresa Resch said. “We set an all-time record of attendance at Montreal and we sold out every single game at Coca-Cola Coliseum. We know that through our brand awareness studies that our brand awareness grew like 75 per cent over the season, which is incredible. ... I would say based on business metrics, our inaugural season was a glowing success.
“But look, anecdotally, the more a team wins the more everything else falls in place."

items: A'ja Wilson wins AP WNBA Player of the Year for 3rd straight year; Angel Reese top defensive player

blocks.text: Resch said the business operations will do a deep-dive on all facets of the business after the season. The basketball department will do the same.

“This is the first of many seasons and we're not going to solve everything in Season 2. It’s about having an understanding about what we need to make a priority and I think that will come with a lot of reflection and be evident quickly," Resch said.

The Tempo ranked last in the WNBA in defensive efficiency — opponents shot a league-best 51.9 per cent against them. That’s not sustainable for success. Some of the defensive issues were injury related but the Tempo desperately need a rim protector and that should be priority No. 1 in free agency over the next two years.
“Not a secret that we need to improve in that area,” general manager Monica Wright Rogers said.

“We were able to chip away at post depth by adding Aneesah [Morrow] before the trade deadline. Adding more opportunities for a post player that can dynamically protect our rim and play the kind of defence that the coaches want to play is the goal.”

The coaching staff and management have consistently stated that they believe Rice will be a standout player in the league. (Full transparency: As an Associated Press WNBA voter, I voted for her on my All-Rookie Team.) Rice’s floor looks to be a quality WNBA starter. What we don’t know yet is whether her ceiling is a WNBA All-Star.
Eye on the WNBA Draft

As important a selection as Rice was, the future of the franchise will be significantly more impacted by this year’s yet-to-be scheduled WNBA Draft. The loss to Connecticut produced a net positive — the Tempo tied for the best lottery odds for the top pick in the Draft.
The jewel prospect is JuJu Watkins, a six-foot-two junior guard for USC who last played 18 months ago after suffering a torn ACL at the end of her sophomore season.
Watkins is considered a franchise-altering generational prospect on the level of Paige Bueckers or Caitlin Clark. But there is a caveat: She has another year of college eligibility if she so chooses.
Give me one good reason Juju Watkins can’t compete in the NBA pic.twitter.com/5SQLolHM3q—Hoopss

The next best prospect is Madison Booker of Texas, a six-foot-one guard/forward who looks to have All-WNBA potential. Notre Dame’s Hannah Hidalgo, a dynamic five-foot-six point guard and Mikaylah Williams, a six-foot guard/forward from LSU are prospects that would be worthy No. 1 selections in other years.
If the Tempo procured Watkins, they would likely be a playoff team next season (injuries permitting). That’s how good her talent is.

The country’s most famous women’s basketball player sees a bright future. Kia Nurse’s on-court future is unclear — she’ll be 31 next year and has broadcasting opportunities ahead of her — but she believes the infrastructure is set up for long-term success.
“We fell short of a couple of our goals here this year – we wanted to be a playoff team,” Nurse said.
“But we put ourselves in a really great place foundationally to build on what we have. Next year everything will not be brand new. ... I think the sky’s the limit, and it’s only up from here.”

articles.title: Hungary lifts PM Peter Magyar’s immunity, clears way for probes into 2 former Orban ministers
articles.summary: Prime Minister Peter Magyar has backed the move himself. Two former ministers who served under his rival Viktor Orban now face separate corruption probes.

image.caption: Magyar, who attended parliament, has described the case against himself as a "farce"Image: Zsolt Szigetvary/MTI/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Hungary's parliament on Monday lifted Prime Minister Peter Magyar's immunity from prosecution, along with that of two former ministers from Viktor Orban's government.
The votes clear the way for investigations involving Magyar and the two opposition lawmakers, who all face separate allegations.
What did the Hungarian lawmakers decide?

Parliament voted 139-0 to lift the immunity of Magyar, former Culture and Innovation Minister Balazs Hanko and former National Development Minister Miklos Sesztak. Lawmakers from Orban's right-wing populist Fidesz party and its conservative Christian Democratic People's Party (KDNP) ally did not take part in the vote.
Magyar, whose center-right Tisza party came to power in April, had himself called on lawmakers to lift his immunity.
Prosecutors are investigating an incident in 2024 in which Magyar allegedly took a mobile phone from a man who was filming him at a Budapest nightclub and threw it into the Danube.
Hungary suspends 'Pro-Orban' public broadcasts
Magyar has described the case as a "farce" and accused prosecutors of trying to associate his case with corruption allegations against former members of Orban's government.
What are the former Orban ministers accused of?
Hanko, now a Fidesz lawmaker, is being investigated over the alleged misuse of public money from Hungary's National Cultural Fund.
Prosecutors allege that public funds were improperly used in more than 1,000 cases, causing losses of 17.3 billion forints (€44.5 million/$52.3 million). Hanko has rejected the allegations.

Sesztak, a KDNP lawmaker who served as national development minister from 2014 to 2018, faces a separate investigation concerning alleged bribes linked to contracts involving the state-owned bus company Volanbusz.
Magyar defeated Orban in April after campaigning on a pledge to investigate alleged corruption and abuses of power during Orban's 16 years in office.
