articles.title: Missing and at risk: Why children in care often run from group homes
articles.summary: For the first time, Nova Scotia is tracking how many youth in care run away. In the last year, group homes have reported hundreds of incidents where youth went missing and were considered at…

image.caption: Grayson Balzan, left, and Ashley Coggins-Comeau both spent time in Nova Scotia's child protection system as children or teens. They want to share their experiences to help children who encounter the system now or in the future. (Cris Monetta and Eric Wiseman/CBC)

blocks.text: Grayson Balzan was only 12 when the last pieces of his childhood were stolen.
A tattered, one-eyed stuffed toy dog named Puppy was one of the few items he took with him to a Dartmouth, N.S., group home when he was placed into government care. He’d had it since he was a baby.
Balzan had Puppy tucked away in his private room when another youth swiped it and hid it. The dog was eventually returned, but the damage was done.
In the first weeks of his stay, he said he remembers other kids in his group home smashing glasses or dishes, ripping posters from walls, throwing food at him, or threatening to fight him.
So he left.
“I would go anywhere, anywhere other than there,” said Balzan, now 21.

For the first time, Nova Scotia is tracking how many youth in care run away like Balzan did. In the last year, group homes have reported hundreds of incidents when youth went missing and were considered at “imminent risk,” a problem the provincial department in charge acknowledges is a major concern.
The numbers come from new quarterly reports compiled by the Department of Opportunities and Social Development that the CBC obtained through a freedom of information request.

Between August 2025 and March 2026, the province tracked hundreds of serious incidents at group homes. Among them, 491 involved a missing child or youth, and it appears from the statistics that some youth are running away repeatedly.
Fewer than 150 children in Nova Scotia live in group homes, suggesting some youth are being reported missing and at risk multiple times.

While serious incidents in group homes have long been reported on an individual level, two years ago Nova Scotia’s auditor general criticized the department for not examining them for "trends or patterns that need to be addressed."

items: Weak oversight of N.S. youth homes increases risk of improper child care: auditor

blocks.text: The department accepted the AG’s recommendation and in the summer of 2025 began doing this quarterly analysis.
Group homes top spot for missing person reports
Lorna Ferguson, an assistant professor of criminology and criminal justice at the University of Regina, believes it’s critical to pay attention to trends of youth being reported missing.
“Missing persons kind of sits at the hub of a lot of social problems in Canada, but yet there's not a lot of attention on it,” said Ferguson, who has written multiple books on the topic.
She said missing youth can be more likely to end up homeless or vulnerable to other dangers like human trafficking.
Ferguson’s research shows group homes are the “number one location” where youth are reported missing, and the place where the most Canadian missing persons reports originate overall.
That’s partly because group homes are required to report missing youth, and often the young person is found safely within hours or returns on their own.
But buried within that larger number are some cases where young people are harmed.

“Any case that goes missing from a group home, because of the pre-existing vulnerabilities for youth in these situations, can have the potential to turn into a harmful or negative experience for the missing person,” said Ferguson.
According to the RCMP’s National Centre for Missing Persons and Unidentified Remains, Nova Scotia police reports list hundreds of “runaway” children each year, with approximately 500 reports in 2025.
An RCMP analysis in 2024 suggested more than half of examined Nova Scotian cases represented “habitual” or “chronic” runaway children and youth.
Why do youth go missing?
Balzan said he left his group home because it never felt like a safe place for him.
Being on the autism spectrum and the youngest in the group home, he said he instantly became a target for bullying and physical violence from older kids.
After the theft of his stuffed animal, he felt he couldn't trust the group home staff.
Balzan said Puppy had been a comfort to him in years when he struggled with sexual abuse and substance abuse in elementary school. The staff said there wasn’t much they could do about the theft.
“I was just really distraught because I was a kid and that was like the only thing I had that was really important to me,” he said.
“I think that was a part of me realizing that, you know, it's nobody but you.”

He was young enough to get on a Halifax Transit bus for free, so he rode around the city and hung out at transit terminals. He wandered in parks at night and sat in the parking area of Dartmouth General Hospital.
One time a strange man picked him up in a car and returned him to the group home. In retrospect Balzan said that was a risky situation for a young child.
“I was just everywhere, just like on the streets,” he said. “But in my mind at that time, it was safer for me instead of being at the group home.”
Balzan said he continued running away from every other group home he was later placed in.
Department deeply concerned

Jill Barkhouse, executive director of the Department of Opportunities and Social Development’s child and family well-being division, said in a recent interview she is “deeply concerned” about the numbers of missing children, and officials are trying to understand them.
“We do work to see the child and youth behind those reports,” Barkhouse said.

The department reaches out directly to the care provider about how to respond to each report. The child’s social worker will also meet the child to figure out what they need or how to keep them safe, she said.

Barkhouse added that children and youth have told the department that life changes can be hard for them. She said often it’s less about running away from their present situation and more about “running to” what is familiar.
Current Nova Scotia social services policy requires group home staff to report to the province if a child is missing no longer than 12 hours from the time they are absent without approval.

The province makes the call on when to report a child’s absence to police, which could happen immediately or up to 24 hours after they are first marked as missing. Many of those reports are received by Halifax Regional Police's vice unit.

"Youth care facilities often automatically report these occurrences as missing persons, as many of these youth are considered vulnerable," Sgt. Gena Graham, the leader of the unit, wrote in an email to CBC.
Not all cases meet the police definition of a missing person case, though, particularly if the young person is still in contact with the home but refuses to return.

Graham said in her experience, some youth leave group homes to go back to their hometowns or be with family and friends. She's also aware of cases where youth have left group homes to use alcohol or drugs.
However, she explained the unit doesn't have the authority to detain a youth unless the group home gets a court order.
Ashley Coggins-Comeau, now 27, said there were many times in her youth when a court order was issued to police directing them to find her.
When she looks up her name on the internet, she still finds pages of results with media stories and missing person reports from more than a decade ago, some with a photo attached.
"So young," she said of those photos. "Then I thought I was old and I knew everything. Looking at it now as an adult is just like: I was a baby."
She estimates staff marked her as “gone without permission” 20 to 30 times.
Looking back, she thinks she might have made different choices if she'd been able to ask for help and guidance.
But she said it was difficult to ask for help and staff often blamed her for leaving, telling her she was "knowingly" putting herself at risk.
She said she had some “amazing” care workers. But with others, she felt judged and disbelieved, and there was little trust between them.
She still feels the impact today.
“I have an issue with trusting people always because of just growing up the way that I did,” she said.
She hopes sharing her story will encourage the public to look closely at the system for children in care, and ask questions about how well it works.
“We all deserve better, and hopefully people start listening,” she said.
‘Their social connections are severed’

Both Coggins-Comeau and Balzan said when they were children, they felt that adults were not listening to them, and they had a limited number of people they could count on while being constantly moved around in the system.
Balzan said he didn’t develop any solid relationships with adults, and said he often felt “looked down on” by the staff working in the system.
There weren’t a lot of constants in Balzan’s life. Before aging out of the care system at 19, he went through six social workers and was moved several times between different group homes and schools.
Coggins-Comeau said she also bounced between various group homes around the province.
When she hears stories of kids being moved between schools and group homes, failing to form bonds, Ferguson sees it as a “severing” of social connections.
That’s important, the criminologist said, because ties to others — even relatively superficial ties — can be the “buffer” that reduces missing incidents and protects children from harm.
“When people are getting moved around and their social connections are severed, that's a risk factor,” she said.
Barkhouse said the department does its best to preserve social connections, and that trust is “key to any relationship.”

She said the department tries to give children stability through supporting group homes and other caregivers to use “trauma-informed practices,” and when change happens, social workers make plans to smooth the transition.
“We do our best to prevent those things from happening and unfortunately it is a reality for some,” she said.
“In many ways, we are trying to keep the losses that children experience to a minimum.”
Aggression, sadness and anger
Balzan feels he’s in a good place in his life now. But he believes the system for children in care failed to help him and worsened his mental health.
He thinks differently about the older youths who bullied him in his first group home.
He is certain they, too, were dealing with past trauma: “Their aggression, their sadness, their very deep-rooted anger,” he said.
“It's just a lot of people that are struggling in one place.”

EDITOR'S NOTE: They are among society's most vulnerable: children who experience traumatic instability and end up in government care. In this series called “Left Behind,” the CBC Atlantic investigative team explores the challenges and outcomes through the eyes of people who lived through this and those trying to help them.

image.caption: Family members and friends of Nepali climbers gather Monday as the bodies recovered after an avalanche on Mount Himlung lie at the morgue of a hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal. (Niranjan Shrestha/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World
Rescue teams on Monday searched for a dozen people swept away by an avalanche that killed at least two others on a Nepalese mountain during severe weather.
Avalanche hit base camp as Nepalis prepared for foreign clients to arrive
Another 10 were rescued from Mount Himlung, a 7,126-metre peak in north-central Nepal after the avalanche hit on Sunday.

All those killed or missing were Nepali nationals. The avalanche hit as they were at a base camp preparing for foreign clients to arrive and climb the peak during the autumn climbing season that began this month.

Helicopters brought down the 10 rescued, while the remains of the two who were killed were airlifted Monday to Kathmandu airport and transported to the Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital. Family and friends were at the hospital morgue but would not comment.

items: Rescuers search for thousands following deadly Nepal-China flood
Woman found alive in home destroyed by Nepal flood, days after family began mourning rites

blocks.text: Flooding and landslides were reported in the Manang district where the mountain is located over the weekend, all caused by heavy rainfall, the district administration office said.
The avalanche comes as the government issued warnings of severe weather all across the entire Himalayan nation.
Nepal's disaster management agency said 21 other people have been killed and five more are missing in different parts of the country between Thursday and Sunday.
Nepal is recovering from devastating flooding in August that swept several villages, leaving more than 1,400 people dead and nearly 6,000 others missing.

articles.title: DepEd, PCMC agreement allows young patients to continue education
articles.summary: Children with long-term health conditions may now continue their education while receiving medical treatment at the Philippine Children"s Medical Center (PCMC) through the Department of Education"s…

blocks.text: Published September 28, 2026 4:43pm

Children with long-term health conditions may now continue their education while receiving medical treatment at the Philippine Children’s Medical Center (PCMC) through the Department of Education’s (DepEd) Alternative Learning System (ALS).

Under a memorandum of agreement between PCMC and DepEd, eligible hospital patients can continue their education through ALS while hospitalized, undergoing treatment, or unable to attend regular school due to prolonged medical care.

Signed on Monday, the ALS program under the agreement included the Basic Literacy Program (BLP), Accreditation and Equivalency (A&E) for Elementary and Junior High School, Regular Junior High School, and Regular Senior High School.
A medical clearance from the attending physician is needed before a patient can undergo ALS.

Eligible learners include hospitalized school-age children, out-of-school children receiving medical care, chronically ill or hospital-bound patients, and long-term patients who are unable to attend formal schooling.

Learning activities will depend on the child’s health condition and treatment schedule. They can learn through modular lessons, bedside instruction, small-group sessions, and blended or online learning.

The Pinyahan Elementary School, Flora A. Ylagan High School, and San Francisco High School will handle the transfer of learner documents and coordinate with PCMC and the Department of Education – Schools Division Office of Quezon City (DepEd QC).
“Going to school may not always be possible for patients with chronic health conditions, but learning does not have to stop,” PCMC Executive Director Dr. Cecilia Gan said.

She also shared that the partnership between PCMC and DepEd marks the first hospital-based learning continuity program in the country, which aims to ensure eligible patients will have continued access to education while receiving medical care. —Mariel Celine Serquiña/RF, GMA News

articles.title: Thai downpours shift north-westwards after Bangkok declared a disaster zone
articles.summary:
Capital city submerged in waist-high flood water, while elsewhere Hurricane Nolo threatens Hawaii’s Big Island

Bangkok was

blocks.text: Bangkok was declared a disaster zone by its city officials towards the end of last week, after streets in Thailand’s capital city were submerged in up to waist-high flood water. The flooding stemmed from an active cell of low pressure across central Thailand that brought continuous heavy rainfall and thunderstorms to Bangkok and surrounding regions.

The heavy rain began early on Thursday when the weak area of low pressure travelled north-westwards up the gulf of Thailand before then sitting over central Thailand by Friday morning. For most of the following two days this low pressure remained roughly in situ, which allowed unrelenting downpours over Bangkok and nearby areas. One weather station near Prachin Buri, just north-east of the capital, recorded 213.5mm within a 24-hour period between Friday and Saturday evening local time – for comparison, London receives an average 585mm a year). Fortunately, the centre of the low-pressure cell shifted north-westwards on Sunday and brought an end to the torrential rainfall.

Out in the central Pacific, meanwhile, citizens of Hawaii’s Big Island were threatened by Hurricane Nolo over the weekend. The system initially approached the archipelago early last week, bringing heavy rainfall from around Tuesday evening. By the early hours of Saturday Nolo was a category 2 hurricane, with sustained windspeeds of 85-90knots (98-104mph), situated at its closest to the archipelago at approximately 145 miles (233km) south of the Big Island. Strong winds were not the only threat to the Big Island, as the vast quantity of rainfall raised concerns over flooding and mudslides. Since the impacts of Nolo started late on Tuesday 22 September, weather stations in the north-east of the island have received over 530mm of rainfall. Fortunately, Nolo has propagated westwards away from Hawaii where it is forecast to peak in its intensity on Monday 28 September, with current predictions of achieving category 4 status.
after newsletter promotion

Meanwhile, farther east in the Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Polo is now forecast to make landfall with the Baja California peninsula late in the day on Monday 28 September. The once category 5 hurricane will downgrade to category 2 by landfall with sustained winds of 96-110mph. A hurricane warning has been issued in coastal regions due to the risk of a storm surge where winds are onshore. Polo will also bring intense downpours while traversing the peninsula with 100-200mm expected, potentially reaching up to 250mm locally. The bulk of this rain falling within a 12-hour period and bringing the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides. The storm will continue to weaken while propagating north-eastwards across the Sonora region in Mexico.

A university in Punjab has suspended classes after protests over a rumored sexual assault took a violent turn. Separately, the Supreme Court has taken suo motu cognizance of recent rape cases in Delhi. DW has more.

blocks.text: Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
September 28, 2026
Lovely Professional University protest: Classes suspended after violence during protests over suspected assault

Punjab's Lovely Professional University (LPU) has suspended classes starting Monday and postponed mid-term examinations after a protest over an alleged rape turned violent on Sunday with protesters clashing with the police and vandalism being reported.

The private university located in the city of Phagwara witnessed massive student unrest after claims spread on social media that a female university student was allegedly raped within the campus premises by an outsider and had later died by suicide.

The protests grew to be violent when the protesters clashed with the police, pelted stones at the security personnel, smashed windows and set fire to some objects within the university complex, reports said.
Some students later claimed in social media posts that the vandals were not students, but outsiders.
Heavy police deployment
The university has suspended regular classes for 10 days, news agency ANI cited a statement from LPU as saying.

The statement said students could travel to their hometowns during the suspension of classes and advised those who stay back to remain in their hostels or places of accommodation and avoid any unnecessary movement. The statement also called on students to avoid involvement in the unrest.
Over 2,000 police personnel were deployed to ensure security on the campus, reports quoted the Additional Director General of Police Fayaz Farooqui as saying.
The protesters also blocked the national highway between Jalandhar and Phagwara highway early Sunday, leading to traffic disruptions.
On Monday, police said that the situation had been brought under control and traffic movement on the highway had been restored.
Claims of rape remain unverified
Meanwhile, the police are yet to confirm whether a student was raped within LPU's campus. They have launched an investigation to examine the facts of the incident.
Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann has taken note of the situation and has directed the Director General of Police to visit the campus, reports said on Monday.
Meanwhile, the Punjab State Women Commision is seeking a detailed report on the alleged rape, ANi reported.
What has LPU said?
The LPU has denied that the alleged rape took place, calling the claims "false, baseless and fabricated rumors".
The university on Sunday posted a video with three female students who it said reside in the girls' hostel room where the alleged incident is claimed to have taken place.
The video purportedly shows the girls denying that there had been a rape, with one of them asking the police to stop visiting the room repeatedly.

However, media reports on Monday said that the same girls later appear in a separate purported video, claiming that they were instructed on what to say in the statement. They then allegedly claim that their clips were "trimmed" and used without their consent.

articles.title: DMW provides psychosocial, livelihood aid to Mary Jane Veloso
articles.summary: The Department of Migrant Workers is providing interventions to former overseas Filipino worker Mary Jane Veloso, including psychosocial and livelihood aid, after she was granted absolute pardon,…

blocks.text: Published September 28, 2026 4:15pm

The Department of Migrant Workers is providing interventions to former overseas Filipino worker Mary Jane Veloso, including psychosocial and livelihood aid, after she was granted absolute pardon, Malacañang said Monday.

“Kasamang sa mga ongoing interventions ng DMW ang psychosocial counseling, livelihood starter kits, enterprise capital at skills training,” Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said during a press briefing.
(Among the ongoing interventions of the DMW are psychosocial counseling, livelihood starter kits, enterprise capital, and skills training.)
“Tiniyak ng ahensya na patuloy ang mga hakbang nito upang masiguro ang maayos na reintegration ni Mary Jane at ng kanyang pamilya sa panibagong yugto ng kanilang buhay,” she added.
(The agency assured that it would continue its efforts to ensure the smooth reintegration of Mary Jane and her family as they begin a new chapter in their lives.)
The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) Field Office 3 earlier provided P30,000 cash aid to Veloso and P10,000 to her parents.
DSWD will also distribute P30,000 each to Veloso’s children today, Castro said.

On Saturday, Veloso returned to her hometown and was warmly welcomed by her friends and family in Barangay Burol, which she had not seen for 16 years. The municipality also gave her a cake and a tarpaulin to mark her personal milestone.

The District Court of Justice of Sieman in Yogjakarta, Indonesia sentenced Veloso to death on October 11, 2010, but it was commuted in 2015 following an appeal from the late President Benigno Simeon "Noynoy" Aquino III.
Veloso maintained that she was innocent and that she was unknowingly used as a drug mule.

In December 2024, Indonesian authorities agreed to transfer Veloso to Philippine custody. She was detained at the Correctional Institution for Women (CIW) in Mandaluyong City, initially serving reclusion perpetua, which carries a prison term of 20 years and one day to 40 years. —Mariel Celine Serquiña/RF, GMA News

articles.title: Anthropic will not appear at Senate inquiry into AI and datacentres amid fallout from OpenAI hack
articles.summary:
Company behind Claude chatbot expected to attend separate Australian government hearing on AI next week

  • Get our

blocks.text: The chief executive of Anthropic will turn down an invitation to appear at a Senate committee hearing on AI this week, in the wake of the revelation that OpenAI agents had breached Australian government websites.
However, the company will make an appearance before another committee early next week.

The chair of the Senate inquiry into AI and datacentres, Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young, wrote to OpenAI and Anthropic last week asking for their US-based chief executives to appear before the committee on Thursday this week.

The invite came after the prime minister’s revelation that OpenAI’s agents had infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia.

Neither company’s executives could be compelled to appear before the Senate committee, given they are based outside Australia, and it is understood that Anthropic – the company behind Claude – will not attend the hearing this week.
It is understood the company’s local team is not in Australia, and the invite was considered last-minute. An alternative date for the hearing has been sought.

Anthropic is, however, expected to attend a separate joint standing committee hearing on AI next week. Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, will not attend, but it is understood representatives of its Australian and US operations will appear.

The company has made a submission to that committee in which Anthropic warned that governments had a critical role in reinforcing a responsible approach to AI by industry, while also arguing that frontier AI was not just an economic capability but also a “national security capability”.
“It matters which countries build the most capable models, and on whose terms they are deployed,” Anthropic said in the submission.

“The most capable AI models are built in the United States. Broadening that development out to trusted allies like Australia is critical and will support efforts to ensure that the capability of democracies outpace those of authoritarian states.”

OpenAI was approached for comment. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, who was in the United States last week when announcing the hack, said he had spoken with OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, “to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident”.

The finance and government services minister, Katy Gallagher, flagged new mandatory reporting rules could be introduced for AI data breaches. After criticism of the government’s slow response to the incident, Services Australia has put in place new procedures to ensure real-time monitoring of information sent to the public-facing email address used by OpenAI to report the hacking.

blocks.caption: ‘We can’t ignore AI or prevent it,’ Anthony Albanese tells UN general assembly – video

blocks.text: But Gallagher rejected Coalition claims the government had politicised the Medicare breach, rejecting suggestions Labor had delayed a public announcement or overstated the significance of the rogue agent’s actions.
after newsletter promotion
“It is the first time that we’re aware that an agent acting on its own, not with the authority of OpenAI, was able to get into one of our data systems, and I think we did the right thing,” she said.
Cabinet was briefed on the ongoing investigation on Monday, as the company continued to cooperate with Services Australia and the intelligence agency, the Australian Signals Directorate.

Gallagher said the investigation would take a matter of weeks to be completed but confirmed the statistical website accessed in the incident had been decommissioned and the data transferred to a new portal.
The taskforce would also review how OpenAI’s agent had interacted with the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare’s website.

An obscure German wiki site that was reportedly hijacked and used as a message board for the agents to communicate with each other included messages showing the agents tried and failed to access the AIHW website data over multiple days in June this year, as first reported by the ABC.
Part of $160m in new funding for cybersecurity improvements at Services Australia, announced in the May budget, will be used for the response to the OpenAI incident.

“The kind of cyber protections of a public-facing website, versus our systems of government significance are quite different, and they are under constant, constant attention from people who would like to get in,” Gallagher said.
“Those systems are the ones that the upgrade will be focused on.”
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said every cyber-attack was serious, but criticised Albanese for waiting to reveal the incident publicly.

articles.title: Can I get AI face? Plastic surgeons say AI-generated inspiration is more than meets the eye
articles.summary: Some plastic surgeons in Canada and elsewhere say they're seeing more people coming in for consultations with AI-modified images of themselves, seeking cosmetic procedures that work that will mirror…

blocks.text: Plastic surgery patients are looking for 'AI face'
Dr. Ian MacArthur is accustomed to dealing with new trends in cosmetic surgery, but he's starting to see more patients coming into his Ottawa clinic with expectations that aren't entirely realistic.
Some clients, he says, bring in "fairly stylized" images generated with artificial intelligence, seeking results that may not even be "physically possible."
The experiences he's had so far motivated him to share a few cautionary thoughts on his Instagram page.
But it's a trend that plastic surgeons are dealing with more often.

The British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (BAAPS) recently warned about the rise of "AI face" — flawless, AI-enhanced images of patients' own faces that they believe can be recreated surgically.
The concern, says the organization's president, is that AI could also lead some people to put their desire for an unachievable look ahead of their own safety and well-being.
"The less realistic the image, the more dangerous that becomes if someone says, 'Yes, I can do it,'" Dr. Nora Nugent told CBC News.
More than meets the AI

BAAPS surveyed about half its roughly 350 members about how often they're seeing instances of AI face during consultations, Nugent said, with about 15 per cent of them responding that it's happening more often.

It's not that people are asking for anything unusual, she says. It's that the chatbot may have made other enhancements that it doesn't immediately disclose, such as a sharpened jawline or smoothed-out skin.

items: Is AI evolving too fast? A look at the debate on slowing it down

blocks.text: CBC News uploaded a photo of a journalist's face to three commonly used generative AI platforms — the free versions of OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google Gemini's Nano Banana and Anthropic's Claude — and prompted them to show the outcome of a rhytidectomy (a facelift).
Claude would not complete the task, responding that it wouldn't generate "realistic manipulated images of actual people."

Nano Banana did complete the task. When prompted, the chatbot explained that in addition to simulating the rhytidectomy, it also reduced loose neck skin and applied dermatological treatments like laser resurfacing or a chemical peel. (It also appeared to shave off facial hair).
It would not, however, create a medical before-and-after image comparison, encouraging consulting with a certified plastic surgeon for a realistic assessment.

ChatGPT did not hesitate to produce a visualization, as well as a side-by-side comparison. Like Nano Banana, it actually simulated multiple procedures — including what appeared to be an eyelid lift, brow lift and neck lift. ChatGPT said it smoothed out the forehead.
The chatbot did not immediately recommend consulting with a surgeon but later said the outcomes depend on one's anatomy, goals and doctor.
Pixels, not human tissue
Nugent says it's important for anyone seeking cosmetic surgery to know that AI can't account for an individual's anatomy.
"[AI] works in pixels, not human tissue," she said.

"Some tissue intrinsically is stronger, has more collagen, maybe thicker skin, and will hold a lift better," she said, adding that there are limits to "what's structurally safe to do" with a person's face.

items: New Brunswick is weaving AI into its K-12 curriculum, drawing praise — and pushback
Canada is investing $150M to make AI safer. Will it work?

blocks.text: "If you make a nose too small and too narrow, that person won't be able to breathe properly through their nose," she said. "If you take too much skin from an eyelid, someone can't close their eyes properly and that creates a medical problem."
On top of that, a patient's age, weight and lifestyle are also factors in the outcome.
AI deepfakes of prominent Canadian doctors are coming for your money
Nugent says people can likely recognize the "more extreme changes" as unrealistic.
"But it's the mild to middle changes that they might think are realistic," she said.

Karen Rowa, a psychiatry and behavioural neurosciences professor at Hamilton's McMaster University, says it could also worsen problems for those who struggle with their appearance or have body dysmorphic disorder.

AI chatbots tend to "please the person they're talking to," she says. Asking them to fix something a person doesn't like about their face or body may "reinforce a problem that may not actually exist."
An unachievable risk
Dr. Michael Weinberg says he hasn't consulted any patients who have used generative AI tools to simulate their cosmetic surgery outcomes, but he's not entirely against the idea.

Weinberg, a plastic surgery division lead at Ontario's Trillium Health Partners, says AI may help a patient visualize their own goals in advance of an appointment. A surgeon can then help them determine what's possible and what's not.
He says plastic surgeons have already been using digital 3D simulation tools in their consultations for some time — for procedures like breast augmentations or eyelid lifts.
"If it's used wisely and judiciously with realistic results, then it is great because it can show you what you can look like," he said.

items: Paging Dr. AI to the ER? Artificial intelligence shows promise in emergency room diagnosis

blocks.text: What he worries about is doctors who overpromise on what can be achieved — whether it's due to inexperience, pressure from the patient or unscrupulous business practices.

"There's a lot of bad plastic surgeons," he said, and a patient's desire to meet AI-generated expectations may lead them to seek less reliable options if they're told that their goals aren't achievable by a more responsible doctor.
He says "tourist plastic surgery" is another issue, with some people travelling abroad for aesthetic procedures.
That comes with a big risk, Weinberg says, of returning with the "absolute worst complications" that can require additional surgeries and months of care.
LISTEN | Just how dangerous is AI — and what we should do about it:
Front Burner33:35Why are AI leaders calling for a slow down?

But Ottawa surgeon MacArthur says most patients are reasonable and aren't looking to go to any extremes. He says those who turn to AI tools may be doing so because they want to better communicate their wishes.

As long as he's clear with them about what is achievable, he says, they're generally understanding. But he does think some people have unrealistic expectations, and that AI could "be like gasoline on the fire."
Why slowing the AI race won't be easy

articles.title: Alcohol is Canada’s biggest drug problem. So why aren’t people getting help?
articles.summary: Research shows alcohol causes more harm overall than any other drug in Canada. Some doctors and other advocates say people struggling with alcohol aren’t getting treatment options that are backed by…

image.caption: Jordan Kawchuk, a writer and former TV producer, recently completed the fifth in-patient program he’s tried during his decades-long struggle with alcohol-use disorder. (Liz Hoath/CBC)

blocks.text: Jordan Kawchuk didn’t imagine having a roommate at the age of 54, let alone more than a dozen of them.
But for six months at the start of 2026, his home was the Vancouver Island Therapeutic Community (VITC), a treatment centre for men in Nanaimo, B.C.

When Kawchuk, a writer and former TV producer, met with CBC’s Audio Documentary Unit during a visit to the treatment centre, he was wearing a blue, button-down shirt, his hair neatly coiffed. He said he often gets mistaken for a member of the staff.
But it was actually his second time at this facility and the fifth in-patient program he’s tried during his decades-long struggle with alcohol-use disorder.

Kawchuk has a long list of things he’s lost to alcohol over the years. He says he’s been fired from countless jobs; he’s lost a lot of money and trust. But he says the hardest part was losing his marriage and the opportunity to live full time with his daughters when they were growing up.
And he’s far from alone. Research shows that alcohol use costs Canadian society around $20 billion a year in health care, lost productivity and criminal justice costs.
Although consumption of alcohol is ticking down slightly overall, according to Statistics Canada, those who do drink are drinking more.

items: We started drinking more during the pandemic — and that habit hasn't changed much, a new survey finds

blocks.text: A national study conducted by researchers from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH), published earlier this year in the Journal of Psychopharmacology, found that alcohol causes more harm overall than any other drug in the country, far more even than non-prescription opioids or tobacco.

The Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI) says around nine people die in Canadian hospitals each day from harm caused by alcohol. Daily hospitalizations for alcohol number 280, compared to 84 for opioids, it says.

On top of that, nearly 18 per cent of people aged 15 years or older in Canada will meet the clinical criteria for an alcohol-use disorder in their lifetime. Still, some doctors and other advocates say people struggling with alcohol aren’t getting treatment options that are backed by science.
Physicians need to do better, addiction doc says
Dr. Evan Ailon is one of them. He runs the only dedicated practice on Vancouver Island for alcohol-use disorder (AUD).
And he says the patients are not usually the hardest part of his job.
“The challenges that I have are with colleagues whose lack of information, lack of knowledge about this really gets in the way of the treatment of these patients.”

Ailon says people seeking help for a problem with alcohol often face stigma and marginalization. His patients tell him that family doctors have ignored their alcohol use or just advised them to cut down.

He says he’s also frustrated that patients are often advised to simply go to Alcoholics Anonymous. While support groups like that do work for some people, they shouldn’t be the only thing offered, he says.

“Some of the most effective medications that have ever been invented in medicine, full-stop, are for alcohol-use disorder, but that is just something that's not known by most providers and certainly not known by the average person.”

Naltrexone, for example, which was approved by Health Canada in 1997, affects the brain’s opioid reward centre, decreasing cravings. It helps people reduce consumption, and for those in recovery, reduces the chance of relapse.
Approved in 2007, Acamprosate improves withdrawal symptoms by restoring balance between the neurotransmitters that get out of whack with chronic alcohol use. It's used to maintain abstinence .
Ailon, who also works in hospitals, says the deaths he sees are often preventable.
“I'll see a patient who comes in with severe liver failure and I can see in the chart that they've had multiple admissions for liver failure…,” says Ailon.
Yet he says he usually finds no mention of treatment for alcohol-use disorder.

“If we as physicians had a patient who came into the hospital with numb feet and a heart attack from very poorly controlled diabetes and we wrote in our charts, ‘this patient continues to eat sugar, despite us telling them they need to stop eating sugar,’ but we've never started them on any of the medications that we have for diabetes, that would be unbelievably unacceptable. Yet for substance use, it's completely normalized.”

items: Life-saving medications for alcohol use disorder 'hugely under-utilized' in B.C., study finds

blocks.text: CAMH says it’s estimated that less than two per cent of people with AUD get appropriate medications.
Jürgen Rehm, a CAMH senior scientist who in 2023 co-chaired a committee that developed new guidelines for treating high-risk drinking, says the condition usually goes unrecognized.

“Because neither the treating physician asks, nor the patient mentions alcohol problems …, overall high-risk drinking, or heavy drinking and alcohol-use disorders, are not being recognized early enough in our health-care system,” said Rehm, who is also a professor at the University of Toronto’s Dalla Lana School of Public Health.
What is driving young Canadians to binge-drink?
‘I’ve seen people roll their eyes’
Jordan Kawchuk has experienced that first hand.

“I've been to emergency rooms where nurses or whoever gives me a stretcher or a bed has said, ‘well, we need this bed for people with more problems than you,’ or I overhear them saying, ‘another bed, another addict, another drunk.’ It's hard even saying that alcohol-use disorder is a disease because I've seen people roll their eyes.”
CBC asked the Canadian Medical Association and the College of Family Physicians of Canada to comment on the state of alcohol treatment in this country, but both organizations declined.
Ailon says he also worries about patients being sent to expensive in-patient treatment programs.
“When I see people who are dropping $40,000 on something that is no better than what they can do as an out-patient, it obviously makes me a little bit hesitant….”
He says he does have patients who were helped by the programs, but it’s important to get to the root of what’s driving alcohol use.

“You can put somebody in a three-month program … but if you, at the end of … those three months, put them back into exactly the same circumstances that they came from that were driving the issue, it's not at all surprising that it doesn't fix the problem.”
Chris Kinch says he agrees in-patient treatment isn’t for everyone. He’s a vice-president at Connective, the non-profit that runs VITC, where Kawchuk has been twice.
Treatment there is free, and he says it works for some people because it’s all about building community.
“So individuals have a highly structured day where they're attending meetings, they're working with each other, holding each other accountable,” Kinch said.
“Community is the method of treatment that's used.”
The men have access to counselling and group therapy. But it's also about teaching them social skills so they can contribute to their communities when they leave treatment, he says.
For Jordan, being in treatment gives him the space he needs to rest, recover and work on himself, he says.
After almost six months at VITC, Jordan says he felt ready to go home in June. His first trip was to visit his daughters in the Okanagan region of B.C.

“I don't care about the careers or getting back to making television or getting rich or owning a home. That's the only thing I want,” he says of fostering a relationship with his kids. “Now it's time to get to know them as adults.”
He says he’s taking his medication, going to AA meetings and writing a book about his struggle with alcohol-use disorder.
“I just have to be diligent. I have to know that it is life and death because the disease is out to kill me.”

articles.title: 'Thrown under the bus': Former defence chief's memoir lays bare his battles with the Trudeau government
articles.summary: Former defence chief Wayne Eyre considered quitting "several times" as he battled the Trudeau government over military misconduct, defence spending and support for Ukraine. His candid memoir recounts…

image.caption: Prime Minister Justin Trudeau shakes hands with Gen. Wayne Eyre, outgoing Chief of the Defence Staff, after his remarks at a change of command ceremony in Ottawa on July 18, 2024. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada's former top military commander considered resigning "several times" during his tenure in battles with the former Trudeau government over the sexual misconduct scandal, and the lack of commitment towards defence spending.

Retired general Wayne Eyre's new memoir, Into the Breach: A Soldier's Journey, also peels back the curtain on the internal debate that took place over how to end the convoy occupation of downtown Ottawa in early 2022.
The prologue to the book, titled The Accidental CDS, is a tongue-in-cheek reference to his unusual, unexpected rise to the position of chief of the defence staff.

Eyre was promoted from being army commander to the top job after now-retired admiral Art MacDonald stepped aside in February 2021 because of allegations of inappropriate behaviour. Those allegations never resulted in charges and MacDonald didn't return to the defence chief's job.
Eyre was left to navigate the wider sexual misconduct scandal and a flurry of allegations which engulfed several high-ranking military leaders — an experience he described as "soul crushing."
He candidly writes about how, in the first few months, he often questioned whether he was up to the task.
Eyre's memoir recounts a highly charged incident in June 2021 where he said he felt thrown "under the bus" by former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland.

At the time, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and Freeland both publicly questioned Eyre's decision to allow the now-former commander of the navy, Vice-Admiral Craig Baines, to remain in his post after he took part in a golf game with former chief of the defence staff Jonathan Vance, who had been under military police investigation following allegations of inappropriate behaviour.
In Eyre's view, Freeland's criticism amounted to forcing the prime minister to choose between his deputy and his senior military adviser.

"If there's no trust between the nation's senior military leader and the nation's senior elected leader, one of them has to go, and it's not going to be the elected leader," Eyre said in an interview with CBC News.
Support from Trudeau kept him from resigning

The incident culminated, Eyre said, when he was on the phone with the prime minister to discuss the decision to retain Baines. He was just about to resign when Trudeau stopped him by saying he still had confidence in him.

After his initial criticism, the prime minister made a further statement of support for his defence chief — remarks Eyre had not seen when the phone call was placed. The crisis was defused, but the tension remained.
Former military commander Eyre says he thought about resigning 'several times'
Eyre served another three years after the incident.
Resignation crossed his mind "several times" as internal battles unfolded over defence funding and the deteriorating state of readiness in the military.
Ultimately, he decided to stay because quitting would have precipitated a further crisis in an already wounded institution.
"You've got to be very careful as a military leader about resigning. You can fall on your sword, but generally it hurts and you can only do it once," he said.

"Resigning is an inherently political act, which could further fray political-military relations, [and] would cause a momentary blip in the media cycle. But at the same time, [it would] cause significant turmoil in the institution."

items: Gen. Wayne Eyre stepping down from position as Canada's top military commander

blocks.text: Throughout his tenure there was a series of rolling crises including the various waves of the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 11, 2022.
At the time, the Trudeau government faced public criticism about its reluctance to approve lethal aid for the embattled Eastern European country. It was a struggle, Eyre acknowledged.
"What we experienced at that time was a collision of ideology with reality," he told CBC.
"The ideology being, we are Canada, we don't supply weapons to a conflict zone. The reality was, OK, this is coming, Ukraine is a friend, this [is] one way we can help."
'Lethargy to approve a new defence policy'

Eyre's book is littered with further examples related to Canada's mission to train Ukraine troops and the transfer of M-777 artillery, underlining his frustration with the government's seeming "inability to make decisions at the speed of war."
He did note there were times when Canada later outstripped its allies in the swift delivery of war supplies and equipment, such as Leopard tanks.
The overall sense of frustration came into sharp focus during Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's September 2023 visit to Canada, which included a series of speeches in Toronto.

items: Zelenskyy's 1st visit to Canada since Russia's war 'emotional,' say some Ukrainians

blocks.text: "Both the PM and Deputy PM Freeland gave bellicose, impassioned speeches about being strong and supporting Ukraine," Eyre wrote, noting the contradiction between the political rhetoric and the fiscal reality that faced the Canadian military at the time.

"I, like the handful of CAF senior leaders present, had a hard time reconciling these otherwise great speeches with both the billion-dollar budget cut that they had just inflicted on us and their lethargy to approve a new defence policy."
The deeper the war in Ukraine became, the more concerned Eyre became about the state of Canada's readiness.
‘Urgency is required,’ says outgoing chief of defence staff Gen. Wayne Eyre on Russia-Ukraine war

He described how, in June 2022, during the run-up to the unveiling of Canada's new policy commitment to NORAD — the by national aerospace command — no one seemed to know where $38 billion in funding was going to come from, or where it would be allocated.

"Most galling was the 'smoke and mirrors' funding approach, with billions already allocated for other military equipment taken away and reallocated, with most investments only coming years into the future," Eyre wrote.
"With confusion persisting several days later, I drew some government ire when I frankly told a journalist that the source of funds 'wasn’t clear to me.'"

items: Top soldier says military looking for 'clarity' on Ottawa's budget plans

blocks.text: Military 'compartmentalized' Ottawa convoy involvement
The memoir also sheds light on a passing reference that appeared in the public hearings related to the invocation of the Emergencies Act to end the convoy protest.

Former deputy defence minister Bill Matthews testified that the military prepared operational plans as a precaution, but they were dismissed due to significant concerns that deploying troops would escalate tensions and mirror the 1990 Oka Crisis.

Throughout the convoy protest crisis, Eyre was firmly opposed to the notion that the military had any sort of role whatsoever. He attempted to correct the public perception by saying there's a difference between planning and scenario spinning.
"We looked at various scenarios, and it wasn't planning because a plan entails assigning troops to task and warning at all levels and the like," Eyre told CBC News.

"No, it was more thinking about various scenarios, and what questions would we have to ask, what measures would have to be taken. But given the sensitivity at the time, it was very compartmentalized."
Most of the discussion, he said, revolved around the use of military tow-trucks to remove protest vehicles.
In his memoir, Eyre wrote: "At the time one of my staff commented, 'If you accomplish nothing else as CDS, keeping the CAF out of this mess is a singular achievement.'"
Canada 'on the right path,' Eyre says
During his final months as defence chief and in his departure speech, Eyre warned about how dangerous the world had become and how Canada needed to prepare.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government reversed many Trudeau-era policies and has begun substantially investing in defence — taking the country to the NATO standard of two per cent of the gross domestic product.

Several European political leaders, as well as security and intelligence agencies have warned that the West is likely to face a major conflict with Russia and possibly even China by the end of the decade.
Asked by CBC whether he thought the country was ready for what may be coming in the next few years, Eyre said no.
"But we're on the right path, and we are getting there."

articles.title: How much would Quebec independence cost? An Alberta study offers clues
articles.summary: With the Parti Québécois leading in the polls and promising a third referendum, the party is facing questions about the economic impact of Quebec independence — and a new study on Alberta separation…

image.caption: If the Parti Québécois wins the Oct. 5 election, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to hold a referendum on Quebec indpendence after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Montreal

With the Parti Québécois leading in the polls and promising a third referendum, the party is facing questions about the economic impact of Quebec independence — and a new study on Alberta separation offers a sobering point of comparison.
Parti Québécois would hold a referendum in 1st mandate if it wins Oct. 5 vote

With the Parti Québécois leading in the polls, the party is facing questions about the economic impact of Quebec independence — and a new study on Alberta separation offers a sobering point of comparison.
If his party forms government, PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to hold a vote on independence after U.S. President Donald Trump's term ends in January 2029.

The delay, St-Pierre Plamondon has argued, is necessary because the unpredictability of Trump's administration would undermine the project. It would be the first time since Jacques Parizeau’s 1994 government that the PQ would take power with the promise to hold a referendum.

The PQ’s 2026 costed platform outlines a $130-million price tag for preparing and holding a referendum. The party's broader Livre bleu — spanning more than 500 pages — paints a rosy picture of independence, and frames separation as a net financial benefit.
"The goal is to end federal waste that duplicates everything we do and loses money like nowhere else, costing us billions of dollars," St-Pierre Plamondon said last month.
According to the document, independence would yield $13 billion to $16 billion in administrative savings by eliminating or merging most of the roughly 230 federal agencies operating in the province.

But the Livre bleu does not fully cover other state expenses, such as establishing an independent military or border services. The PQ contends it would maintain an open border with Canada and reroute tax money currently directed to the Canadian military at no extra cost.
A $170B cautionary tale
A recent report examining the possibility of an independent Alberta, however, presents a more complex economic reality.

The report, commissioned by the Alberta government and conducted by experts at the University of Calgary, found that Alberta’s separation from Canada could cost between $50 billion and $170 billion over a five-year period.
It's hard to see the economic upside from Quebec independence.- Tim Sargent, University of Calgary

It lays out two possible scenarios — a “smooth” option, in which negotiations to exit Canada would be quick and favourable to Alberta, and a “difficult” option, in which those negotiations would drag on and be unfavourable to the province.
Tim Sargent, the lead economist on the report, said in an interview that the cost to the Quebec economy and its finances would likely be comparable.

"It's hard to see the economic upside from Quebec independence," said Sargent, a longtime economic expert in the federal civil service and the director of economic growth and prosperity at University of Calgary's school of public policy.
"It wouldn't be hard for me to see losses in GDP, maybe not quite as high as we have for Alberta, but — choose my words carefully here — a similar order of magnitude is not unreasonable."

items: The tangled what-ifs of Alberta separation
With time running out, new poll suggests Alberta separatism support is slipping

blocks.text: In terms of the province's finances, he said a sovereign Quebec would "face a bigger risk premium" that would increase interest rates throughout the economy. This could be passed on to consumers, raising interest rates on people's mortgages and lines of credit.

He acknowledged that Quebec's setup costs would be lower because it already has institutions like Revenu Québec and the Quebec Pension Plan. But he pointed out that, unlike Alberta, Quebec doesn't have an oil and gas sector it could unleash for potential economic gain.
The Brexit comparison
Sargent noted that exports to the rest of Canada account for about 20 per cent of both provinces' GDP.
He said turning an interprovincial border into an international one could slow down that trade, pointing to the economic slowdown in the United Kingdom after it left the European Union.
"If you look at what happened after Brexit, the U.K.'s goods exports went down significantly," Sargent said.
"You could no longer just drive stuff from Dover to Calais without having to fill in any forms. And it would be the same if Quebec left."

items: Alberta separation too costly with too many uncertainties, warns Calgary think-tank

blocks.text: The University of Calgary report, which was reviewed by an independent panel, cites historical studies conducted in Quebec prior to the 1995 referendum that projected a real GDP contraction for the province ranging between 1.2 per cent and 7.7 per cent.
The authors also point to Quebec's 1980 referendum period as a precedent for corporate head office relocations driven by political uncertainty.
The report relies on historical research because independent economic analysis on Quebec independence virtually dried up after the 1995 referendum, Sargent said.
Quebec Conservative leader rules out referendum in balance-of-power scenario
Uncertainty the operative word
Daniel Béland, director of the McGill Institute for the Study of Canada, said the Alberta study highlights a key element about any secession project: uncertainty.
(Another recent Alberta study, produced by a pro-independence group, found that an independent Alberta would have a potential budget surplus of as much as $32 billion a year. )

"There are so many different factors that can affect the cost of the transition," Béland said, pointing to questions around the state of the economy, international recognition of a newly formed state and negotiations with Canada.
"It's a process that can take years," he added. "It's hard to put an actual number on it, but it's good to have this exercise."
With Quebecers heading to the polls on Oct. 5, Quebec independence could become a greater target for St-Pierre Plamondon's rivals, Béland said.

items: Compare the promises of Quebec’s major parties in the 2026 election

blocks.text: During Wednesday's debate, both Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette and Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard argued a referendum would lead to economic turmoil.
In defending his position, St-Pierre Plamondon has described himself as an "optimist" and on the side of "courage and hope."
"We shouldn't be afraid of democracy," he said during Wednesday's debate. "Jacques Parizeau used to say, 'Don't be afraid of your democracy, of going to the polls, of reflecting on our future.'"
Why the greater Quebec City area could play a big role in this election

articles.title: How police balance surveillance with public safety in investigations like Project South
articles.summary: Some of the Toronto police officers charged in the Project South corruption probe were allegedly seen drinking and doing drugs in their vehicles while under surveillance. Determining when to…

image.caption: Project South investigators observed Barnhardt and Const. Saurabjit Bedi in this Walmart parking lot in Brampton, Ont., last October, according to an information to obtain application. (Grant Linton/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto

Some of the Toronto police officers charged in the Project South corruption probe were allegedly seen drinking and doing drugs in their vehicles while under surveillance. Determining when to intervene in these kinds of scenarios is a balancing act, say experts, but public safety is always the "paramount consideration" for investigators.
Officers charged in corruption probe seen drinking, doing drugs in vehicles: court document
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 28, 2026 4:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 2 hours ago
Cops charged in Project South allegedly seen drinking, doing drugs in vehicles
Last October, Toronto police Const. Timothy Barnhardt and Const. Saurabjit Bedi met up in a Walmart parking lot where Barnhardt allegedly sold Bedi a "ball" of cocaine.
Project South investigators were watching.

The two officers were also observed drinking alcohol and snorting lines of cocaine in Barnhardt's Jeep Wrangler while discussing selling drugs, and the effects and purity of the cocaine they'd just ingested, according to an information to obtain (ITO) application in the sweeping corruption probe.

That meeting in Brampton, Ont., is one of at least nine instances detailed in the ITO during which police officers charged in Project South were observed consuming drugs or alcohol inside a vehicle between early October and the end of December 2025.

The application doesn't say whether investigators believed the officers were impaired following these incidents or what — if any — steps they took to protect the public if investigators suspected the officers would drive away impaired.

However, there are at least three other occasions outlined in the ITO when investigators warned members of the public they might be targeted by criminals based on Project South surveillance and created safety plans with them.

So how do police decide when to intervene and potentially blow a surveillance operation in order to protect the public? It's a balancing act. Sometimes officers can step in and still maintain the integrity of the investigation but, experts say, public safety is the "paramount consideration."

"If public safety is potentially being compromised, you don't have a choice. You've got to jump in there," said Hank Idsinga, a retired Toronto homicide detective who recently published a memoir on his career.
"You've got to intercede and make sure something doesn't happen where somebody could be injured or killed."

Project South began in June 2025 when York Regional Police thwarted an alleged plot to kill a senior corrections officer at Toronto South Detention Centre. While investigating, York police discovered that Barnhardt had allegedly shared confidential information about that correctional officer with a civilian.
From there, investigators expanded the scope of the probe to look into Barnhardt and others' ongoing alleged criminal activity, including drug trafficking, through wiretaps and surveillance.

The charges against Barnhardt, Bedi and other officers and civilians accused in Project South have not yet been tested in court. Barnhardt's lawyer previously declined to comment on the ITO allegations, and Bedi's did not respond to a request for comment.
'Primary consideration'

In a statement, a York Regional Police spokesperson told CBC News "public safety remained a primary consideration throughout Project South" but would not comment on the steps and techniques investigators used while charges remain before the courts.
Idsinga was involved in — and oversaw — many wiretap projects during his 35-year policing career, which included 18 years with Toronto's homicide squad.
"The minute those wiretaps go up, you start intercepting calls, you're intercepting evidence of criminal behaviour on a daily basis, and it's up to you to decide what to do about it," he said.
For example, Idsinga says if he heard about gun trafficking, officers would have to step in to make sure the gun was never used on the street.

But as soon as police make an arrest the "disclosure clock starts ticking" and, he says, part of that disclosure would be that investigators intercepted a call on a wiretap — alerting the suspects that police are listening.
"If that compromises your wiretap investigation, so be it," said Idsinga.

items: 'Cocaine eyes' to cash bribes: 5 revelations from Project South wiretaps
Toronto cop charged in Project South allegedly didn't care if selling information harmed people

blocks.text: Speaking generally, criminal lawyer David Butt says police liability is always front and centre in these decisions. Under the Community Safety and Policing Act in Ontario, officers have an "affirmative sworn duty to protect the public."

"You can protect the public by large and complex investigations, you can protect the public by arresting impaired drivers," Butt, who has represented both police officers and victims of crime, told CBC News.
"The point being, that recklessly or unreasonably failing to do either one of those does put [police] in jeopardy of being found liable."

Sometimes, Butt says, it's possible for officers to preserve both interests, such as by having a front-line officer independently observe the alleged impaired driving, or by arresting the suspect to take the risk off the road, but then asking the Crown not to prosecute to avoid disclosure.
"That's perhaps the best trade-off that preserves the bigger investigation," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nicole Brockbank is a reporter for CBC Toronto's Enterprise Unit. She digs up, researches and reports GTA-focused investigative and enterprise stories. nicole.brockbank@cbc.ca

articles.title: First Nation chiefs call for Indigenous-led search unit for missing persons in northern Ontario
articles.summary: First Nation leaders in northern Ontario are calling for the launch of an Indigenous-led search-and-rescue pilot program after five missing people were found dead in Thunder Bay this spring. Three of…

image.caption: An area by the Neebing-McIntyre Floodway in Thunder Bay, Ont., is seen taped off by police on May 21. Five people reported missing were found dead in the city this spring. (Sarah Law/CBC) (Sarah Law/CBC)

blocks.text: Thunder Bay

First Nation leaders in northern Ontario are calling for the launch of an Indigenous-led search-and-rescue pilot program after five missing people were found dead in Thunder Bay this spring. Three of them were members of Nishnawbe Aski Nation communities. At their annual Keewaywin Conference, chiefs voted in favour of a NAN search-and-rescue pilot project. Here's what that could look like.
5 reported missing were found dead in Thunder Bay this spring
WARNING: This story contains references to missing and murdered Indigenous people. Resources can be found at the bottom of this story.

First Nation leaders across northern Ontario are calling for the launch of an Indigenous-led search-and-rescue pilot program after five missing people — three from Nishnawbe Aski Nation (NAN) communities — were found dead in Thunder Bay this spring.

During their annual Keewaywin Conference on Thursday, chiefs with NAN, a political-territorial organization that represents 49 First Nations across Treaties 9 and 5, voted in favour of a NAN search-and-rescue pilot project.

The program, which would be called NAN SAR, would provide search co-ordination, trained search personnel and volunteers, family support, crisis response and other assistance when NAN members are reported missing in the region.
NAN itself cannot operate such a program due to its mandate as a political-territorial organization; however, it has committed to support a designated operator to lead this work.

“We can no longer just 100 per cent rely on the Thunder Bay police or other bodies that are out there,” said NAN Grand Chief Alvin Fiddler ahead of Thursday’s vote. “We need to create our own body to do this work.

“The system as it currently exists, it is not respectful to the family, it's not respectful to our communities, it is not respectful to the volunteers that come from our communities to assist in these search efforts.”
There is no estimated timeline for when NAN SAR could be up and running.
Disappearances, deaths in matter of weeks
NAN communities continue to mourn the deaths of Ashlynn Bottle, 23, Nodin Skunk, 25, and Kelsey Anderson, 36.
The TBPS faced heavy backlash as a result of these cases, with First Nation searchers saying their input and traditional search practices weren’t taken seriously by the force.

Bottle and Skunk, members of Mishkeegogamang First Nation, were last seen together at the old Pool 8 grain elevator on the city’s south side on April 26. The Thunder Bay Police Service (TBPS) confirmed they were no longer considered missing on May 15.
First Nation leaders have told CBC News that searchers from Cat Lake First Nation found the two dead inside the grain elevator.

Kelsey Anderson, 36, was last seen on May 9 in the Thunder Centre shopping area. He grew up in Kasabonika Lake First Nation, was a member of Webequie First Nation and also had ties to Nibinamik First Nation.
The TBPS announced on May 25 that Anderson was no longer considered missing and later confirmed a 33-year-old Thunder Bay man was charged with manslaughter in connection with his death.
During a community-led effort for Anderson, searchers found the remains of 42-year-old Thunder Bay resident Richard Graham, who was reported missing in summer 2024.
Chief Matthias Anderson of Kasabonika Lake First Nation shared his frustrations during Thursday’s Keewaywin Conference.
“There are so many players involved when it comes to finding a missing person and that there is a lot of miscommunication going around,” he said.
Police chief welcomes NAN SAR concept

Thunder Bay police Chief Darcy Fleury told CBC News on Friday that he’d welcome a NAN SAR pilot program in the city, and acknowledges the importance of Indigenous knowledge during searches for missing people.

“That's great to have that as another resource for the community,” Fleury said. “The Thunder Bay Police Service is responsible for search and rescue in the city, so we welcome that approach that they're taking to have trained volunteers to come in and give us a hand.”

Fleury said he spoke with NAN leaders this summer to discuss their concerns, adding it’s important for police and community search groups to be on the same page about expectations, roles and responsibilities, and what kind of information can be shared publicly during active investigations — especially criminal matters.
“They've identified it, we've identified it, that lack of communication."

items: Manslaughter charge laid in Thunder Bay, Ont., in connection with missing persons case
First Nations say they're being disrespected as tension rises with Thunder Bay police over missing persons

blocks.text: The Broken Trust Report released by Ontario's Office of the Independent Police Review Director in 2018 found evidence of systemic racism within the force

Since then, the force has been working on strengthening relationships with Indigenous leaders and groups to rebuild trust, including incorporating input from Indigenous partners into its missing-persons procedures, Fleury said.
Provincial review of TBPS ongoing

It’s been almost two years since Ontario’s inspector general of policing, Ryan Teschner, announced he would evaluate how the TBPS conducts death and missing-person investigations, as well as its compliance with the province's policing legislation.
The review was spurred by “several complaints” about the TBPS that were filed with the provincial Inspectorate of Policing, Teschner told CBC's Up North.

items: Families of 2 men separately reported missing in Thunder Bay, Ont., say they're grieving
Members of several First Nations searching for missing man in Thunder Bay, Ont.

blocks.text: CBC News has reached out to the Inspectorate of Policing for an update on the review and is awaiting a response.

In February, a spokesperson said the Findings Report was being developed and expected to be released in the coming months. Teschner will then determine whether there’s been any non-compliance with the Community Safety and Policing Act and direct the TBPS accordingly.

Support is available for anyone affected by the issue of missing and murdered Indigenous people. Immediate emotional assistance and crisis support is available 24/7 through a national hotline at 1-844-413-6649.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Sarah Law is a CBC News reporter based in Thunder Bay, Ont., and has also worked for newspapers and online publications elsewhere in the province. Have a story tip? You can reach her at sarah.law@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Trump-Xi summit: What wasn't said might matter the most
articles.summary: The most revealing thing about the summit in Washington may be what the two leaders did not say - and what we still don't know.

blocks.text: Chinese state media confirmed for the first time on Monday that the trade truce has been extended until 10 January.
The short extension ensures both leaders will meet again at major international gatherings later this year.
Trump will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November while Xi is due to travel to Miami for the G20 summit in December.
It is rare for the leaders of the world's two largest economies to meet so frequently.
But Beijing had hoped for a much longer extension to the truce, making the two month reprieve a modest gain rather than a major breakthrough.
China did secure lower tariffs on $30bn (£23bn) of goods entering the US with reciprocal reductions expected from Beijing.
Chinese products heading to American stores ranging from toys to small household appliances to Christmas decorations will benefit from the lower tariffs.
The Trump administration also said Beijing would buy at least 10 million metric tons of coal annually in 2027 and 2028.
What is striking is what was left out.
There was no mention of increasing exports of China's rare earth minerals to the US nor was there any indication that restrictions on advanced US semiconductors would be eased.
The White House factsheet made no mention of Taiwan, but the issue was clearly a priority for Xi Jinping.
According to Beijing's accounts of the talks, Xi urged Donald Trump to formally oppose Taiwan independence and handle the issue with caution.
After their previous meeting in May, Trump revealed that Xi directly asked him if the US would defend Taiwan in the event of a Chinese attack.
He told reporters, "There's only one person that knows that, and it is me," and he raised the question whether it made sense for US forces to "travel 9,500 miles to fight a war" over the issue.
This time, Trump disclosed far less.
"We didn't talk about it too much," he told reporters over the weekend.
"Right now, it's fine. It's just moving along," Trump said. "He understands very much how I feel."
That silence may be significant.
Trump has previously described a proposed $14bn US arms package for Taiwan as "a very good negotiating chip" in his dealings with Beijing. The arms package has been on hold for months.
Adding to the confusion, US Ambassador to China David Perdue told Fox News that Trump had offered to sell weapons to Xi during the summit.
The State Department later clarified that US law prohibits arms sales to China and there are no plans to do so.

Beijing sees the self-governing island as part of China. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

China says it will allow more foreign financial firms, including American-backed banks, investment companies and insurers, to apply to do business and open offices in China. But any approvals will still be subject to Chinese laws and regulations.
The last line is key. China is opening the door, but still controls who gets through it.

Foreign financial firms have long complained that regulatory barriers, licensing requirements and concerns over exit bans make it difficult to expand in China, even when market access is technically allowed.
Beijing also said it was discussing ways to increase the number of flights between both countries, but neither side has explained how this would happen.
And despite giving visa free entry to visitors from more than 75 countries across the world, China has not extended that offer to Americans.

Meanwhile the US State Department continues to classify travel to China as a Level 2 advisory urging travellers to "exercise increased caution" because of the risk of arbitrary law enforcement, exit bans and detention.
So even though both sides are talking about encouraging business and travel some of the biggest obstacles remain firmly in place.

And that’s as far as I wish to go this morning.

blocks.text: Police investigate possible Iran link to suspected bomb plot

Good morning and welcome to our coverage of events at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire as counter-terrorism police investigate whether Iran is behind a suspected bomb plot at the base which is used by the US military to carry out missions in the Middle East.
Five men detained near the base early on Sunday were initially detained over explosives offences and then were further arrested later in the day on suspicion of the preparation of a terrorist act.

It came after armed officers found explosives on three vans parked minutes from the base. The suspected plot appears to have been foiled by chance when a local farmer spotted unusual behaviour late at night in the countryside from a group of men and called 999.
Dozens of households in the Cotswolds village of Whelford were subsequently evacuated during the operation and have still not returned to their home. Stay with us for further developments.
